It was believed that the gods gave us our gifts, but that it was up to us to push fate along and achieve our full potential. The waste of talent was a great source of sadness to the Norse. One did not squander good health, a good pair of hands or an inclination towards poetry, music or service to the gods.

cards.name: Laguz
cards.up:
Do not push forward. Do not force the issue. There is a time and place for everything. Allow things to come to you, now. Be refreshed by a slower pace. Allow yourself to dream. Use your imagination more fully.
I float upon the waters,
Supported, and I feel
The ripples of
Everything.
I ripple back to
Everything,
And there is more,
And I flow closer,
And it is all beautiful
And wise.
I am Laguz.
Water could be seen as the dominant element in the Norse world. The Vikings sailed upon it, extending their empire and becoming masters of the seas. The oceans, rivers and lakes connected them with the rest of the world, and they harvested – benefited from – the riches they found in those bodies of water. For instance, the simple art of drying cod enabled the Vikings to be at sea or off exploring new lands for extended periods of time, because the long lasting staple ensured they could eat even when other food supplies were depleted.
The Norse also watched the landscape changing from green to white, as winter snows and ice advanced and even the waterfalls froze solid. These conditions of the changing element of water dictated how they lived and where (and when) they travelled.
Laguz (pronounced, "law-gooze") is the rune of the waters or lake. It concerns itself with imagination and dreaming. It suggests we allow things to flow to us, rather than aggressively going after them. The saying "still waters run deep" could have been written for this rune, as it suggests we should allow ourselves to delve deeply into our emotions and our dreams to discover their pleasures and wisdom.
Laguz carries a deeply spiritual energy, one that asks us to connect with the more intuitive and even psychic aspects of ourselves. It asks us to feel our way, rather than to think our way forward.

cards.name: Inguz
cards.up:
Profound strength grows slowly. Do not take shortcuts. Make use of stored power. The positive power of the masculine is available for all. Take action and learn by doing.
Slow and steady,
Like a sapling growing to be
The great tree with roots that
Run deep
Grounded
That no wind can reap,
No storm can touch,
Magic starts here, ready.
I am Inguz.
Inguz is the rune of the masculine divine and represents the active "doing" power of the masculine. It advises that its fertile and explosive power is available to us – that if we store our strength and energy over time, we can release it towards something we want. Inguz (pronounced, "ing-waaz") is both a powerful rune of manifestation and an expression of the moment of powerful centring before that manifestation is invoked.
It also reminds us that we build strength over time. For instance, when we first go to a gym, we don't attempt to lift a barbell that weighs more than we do! Even if we can shift it, we are likely to hurt ourselves in the process. Eventually, of course, we work up to it, and may be able to lift that weight and more. But we have to ready our body by putting in the time to increase its strength.
This gradual increase of strength is applicable to our mind and mental powers as well as to our body and physical powers. Mentally, we develop the focus needed to complete a difficult process or task in the same way that we develop physical strength in the gym.
Inguz can be used as a fertility talisman for both men and women and was a symbol of the male mysteries in Viking society.

cards.name: Dagaz
cards.up:
Know that you are protected. Only positive energy flows your way. Expressing daily gratitude will create profound change. Have hope! Happiness is within your grasp – the time for sorrow is over. Grief is necessary, but soon will diminish. Seek balance in all things.
The darkness is complete,
Until it is not.
The black is no longer black,
But blue, and then
Purple, then streaked
With pink,
Orange, yellow, gold.
Warmth, hope,
Happiness.
All is changed.
I am Dagaz.
Dagaz (pronounced, "daa-gahz") is a rune in the Elder Futark that says good things have arrived or are coming soon. It is the rune of the miracle of the dawn, the coming of the day, the first rays of sunlight after a frightening storm. It is the awakening of hope when it seemed hope was gone. It is the first gentle happiness after a period of grieving, the understanding that we can choose pleasure after a period of sacrifice. It is the relief after much hard work.
Dagaz is a protective force, too. It enhances happiness by warding off anything that may challenge that happy state. It is useful in dispelling depression, inducing hope and bringing forth a balanced mind and body. Dagaz was painted in yellow on the doorways of halls, where happy events were held, ensuring not only that good times would be had, but that the people within would be protected from harm while enjoying themselves.

cards.name: Othila
cards.up:
Equilibrium. Things will stay as they are. We are rich if we have our family, our friends and our health. Ancestral energy becomes important. A gift of inheritance may be forthcoming.
I am the result
Of a thousand lifetimes
Of love,
Of bravery,
Of tears,
Of joy,
Of skills,
Of connection:
The bloodlines that flow.
I am Othila.
For the Vikings, ancestor worship was an important aspect of their spiritual tradition. Forebears and bloodline were a very important part of a Viking's identity and contributed to their sense of their own inherent power. Descendants kept particularly beloved ancestors "alive" by naming children after them. The Norse also prayed to ancestors for guidance and kept their burial mounds well tended. The dead were often buried near to the living so as to keep them close to their families.
At memorial feasts, one by one guests would drink memorial toasts, called minni, to honour the life and energy of the recently deceased. In this way, the Norse believed they honoured the dead enough to receive continued help after their family member's passing. The deceased were said to give the living good advice when consulted, help with the fertility of the land and animals and chase away negative energies.
Othila (pronounced, "aw-theel-law") is the rune of ancestors and family. It speaks to relationships, suggesting that if you have good relationships with those around you, particularly your blood kin, as well as a good relationship with your own body – your health – you are as rich as if you had chests of gold.
This rune asks us to see that, even if we dislike members of our family for good reason (they may actively have hurt us), in our blood and DNA we carry positive aspects of our ancestors. Our forebears may be responsible for a particularly beautiful physical feature we possess or our ability to easily pick up a certain skill or our musicality or creativity. Whether or not we are aware of which ancestor passed on a particular gift, Othila reminds us to be thankful to our ancestral line for the gifts we have received from our forebears.

cards.name: The Void
cards.up:
Possibility. Still undecided by the gods. Things in flux. A little mystery is a positive thing. Knowing that we don’t know is a great place from which to begin to learn. There is great potential in your current position. The fate of this issue is not yet decided.
The fallow field,
The burial mound after all have gone,
The slate after the wind,
The broom after work,
The midnight sun,
The clear wind,
The empty seedpod,
The snow as it falls upon itself,
I am the Void.
The Void, represented as a blank stone or piece of wood, was included to remind us that sometimes not knowing is the best way forward. Whilst not part of the Elder Futhark, it grew to be a part of the metaphysical and divinatory processes. But the Void does not mean absolute emptiness. Rather, it suggests that fate has not yet decided about the subject presented. It may also mean that the way is completely open to our own will and creative force. "Yes", it says. "The way is open, and it is all up to you!" This may be both a welcome message and a daunting one. 
Consider a fallow field: It breathes and rests, yes, but it is not truly empty. It is full of the good earth waiting for the seeds to be laid within it. It is waiting to support new growth, to create. Like the fallow field, the Void, too, looks empty. But it is, in fact, full of possibility and choice.

cards.name: Fenrir
cards.up:
There is power in endings. Let go of your hatred. Belittling others to make yourself feel superior is never wise. Do not automatically fear those whom you may not fully understand. First impressions are not always correct.
I am ravenous.
My mouth open,
The yaw lined with great white teeth.
I chase the light.
I eat, too, the darkness you offer.
My eyes see all.
Yes, even you.
And I taste the flesh of the betrayers.
I wait.
Soon.
Vikings both greatly admired and greatly feared the wolf. An apex predator, wolves not only competed with the Norse peoples for wild prey, they also killed farmers' livestock and ate the flesh of dead warriors left on the battlefield. Yet these same animals were understood to be protective, family oriented and to play an important role in maintaining the ecological balance.
While Odin's Hall, the haven of Valhalla, was guarded by wolves, perhaps the most frightening of all Norse images of destruction is that of the giant wolf Fenrir eating the moon and sky at Ragnarok. Also, Sol and Mani (sun and moon) were said to have been chased by two wolves, one called Hati (Hate) and the other called Skoll (Mockery), sons of the fearsome Fenrir. (This presents us with a mythos where two light-bringing deities, Sol and Mani, are constantly threatened by two dark emotions, hate and mockery – a good indication of how the Norse felt about the value of those emotions!)
However, it is Fenrir, in another key mythos, who is seen to be betrayed. It was prophesied that three of Loki's children would destroy the world at Ragnarok. When Fenrir and his two siblings – a serpent named Jörmungandr and the giantess Hel – were seen to grow more powerful each day, the gods began to worry. Odin asked they all be brought to him. Then Odin threw Jörmungandr into "that deep sea that lies round all lands", and Hel was given the realm of Helheim, from whence she could not escape.
This left Fenrir for the gods to deal with. The gods approached Fenrir, telling him they wanted to test the strength of some bindings against his powers. Fenrir, who was suspicious, said they could do so, but only if one of the gods put their right hand into his mouth for "insurance." The god Tyr volunteered. He put his hand into the huge jaws of Fenrir, and when the gods bound Fenrir fast to a huge stone, Fenrir bit off Tyr's hand. While we can sympathise with the gods for trying to save their world, we can also feel the justice in Fenrir's savage reaction. (Ultimately, Fenrir killed Odin at Ragnarok, after the mighty stone to which he was bound smashed in an earthquake.)
The Norse knew we should never allow the wolves of hate, mockery or suspicion run free in our lives. Therefore, we should refrain from automatically fearing that which we don't understand and seek to understand those who are different from ourselves.

cards.name: Freyja
cards.up:
Birth and death are both part of life. Feminine power is different from but equal to masculine power. You can fight your own battles. Choose partners with discernment. Fertility in all forms surrounds you now. Healing in body, mind and spirit is currently available to you. External beauty is rarely enough – seek depth and intelligence, too.
All maidens and mothers,
Come to me
Invoke my name in wisdom
All warriors seek me out
Magic flows from my body
A treasure beyond the gold I wear
I am equal, powerful, flowful
Fertile,
I am Freyja.
Picture the most beautiful warrior woman standing naked upon a battlefield, hair whipping around her, head high, eyes flashing, weapons bloodied. Between her breasts, a magnificent gold and amber necklace glitters. Despite the death and chaos around her, men cannot take their eyes from her – they both fear and desire the mighty goddess Freyja.
Freyja is known as the defender of women, a battle queen, healer and a deity of birth and death, war, witchcraft and fertility. She is often depicted naked, unabashed in her power and primal sexuality, wearing nothing but the great constellation of a necklace called Brisingamen (fire). Wrought from gold and amber, Brisingamen is said to represent the power of the four elements and the fertile power of the synergy of these elements, together. When Freyja dons her necklace, she is irresistible to all!
Within the Norse mythos, Freyja is equal in status to the Allfather Odin. In battle, she gets half the slain and Odin, the other half. Her maidens, known as the Valkyries, assist Freyja in removing the heroic dead from the battlefield. Even after death, men desire Freyja and long to be in her hall and fight by her side at Ragnarok.
Freyja is known for her wisdom as well as for her lustful nature. Norse women sought her blessings and advice on healing and on magic and sexual matters. Women hoped to enter her hall after death, and many grave rune stones mention that the woman went to Freyja.

cards.name: Fripgeard
cards.up:
It is time to find refuge. We all need occasional respite from the chaos and pressure of the world around us. There is profound sanctity in places that protect us. Silence is valuable, now. Secure both the protection of your community and your own peace. Seek the action that will weave peace into the current situation.
In the quiet shade of the great tree,
I can lay down my sword,
I can put down my shield.
As your strong shield arm is about me,
Here under your gaze all is well.
Woven into each stone and ray of sunshine
Is friþgeard,
And I claim peace.
The Viking friþgeard was a place dedicated to the gods and was sacred to nature spirits, like elves, as well. Located near trees, springs, stones and other natural spots that were considered to be receptacles of great magical power, these were places the community or kinship group went to worship.
While access to some of these sacred places was restricted to those of a certain rank or religious status, most were available to all members of the community – even oath breakers. There were, however, guidelines assuring there would be no hunting, harvest or cultivation in these areas – and of course no blood spilled. Breaking the boundaries of the friþgeard was a serious matter, the punishment for which could include death or exile.
Kinship was of prime importance to the Vikings, which meant that peaceful relations and strong bonds within families and kinship groups was important, too. When a woman married into another family group she was referred to as a "frith-weaver", as she was seen as knitting together her and her husband's families as kin, as well as providing the living links of children.
The source word, "frid" (Old Norse, "fridr"), means a state of non-disturbance, so the concept of friþgeard can be applied as a state of mind, as well as a place. As a mental state, it suggests peace, protection and loyalty.
Should this card come to your attention, look for a peaceful way forward. Since peace comes from within, seek to understand what may be disrupting your peace. Create a place of peaceful sanctuary to support your inner sense of peace.

cards.name: Hel
cards.up:
Things are not always as they seem. Death is only the beginning. Keep moving through difficult circumstances – don’t get stuck. You may need to rest at the end of a long project or difficult time. You may receive an inheritance of some kind.
I walk towards a place of rest.
The road is long,
The sun is setting,
I have my shoes, and
I know it is time
To pause and allow my name
To be given elsewhere,
Until my time to see the dawn again.
Hel is both a place name and the name of a jotun (giant/ess), a daughter of the god Loki. It was Hel the giantess who created the Hel that is one of the three realms situated under the roots of the world tree, Yggdrasil. But do not confuse the Norse concept of Hel with the Christian Hell. Hel is not a terrible place of fire and brimstone – instead, it’s a peaceful, rather cold place. However, Hel wasn’t seen to hold the same status as Odin’s or Freyja’s halls, Valhalla or Fólkvangr. Rather, Hel was where humans went after a death that was neither particularly brave nor courageous. Therefore, Hel the giantess received a portion of the dead, just as Odin and Freyja did.
The dead were imagined as having to walk a long road to get to Hel. Women might have gotten a wagon to ride in, but most walked. The road to Hel was seen as a middle place, somewhere you didn’t want to be stuck. The road was tough, and it was a reward in itself to get safely to Hel.
If you were going to walk to Hel (and possibly back), you ought to be wearing strong, comfortable shoes because you didn’t want to be stuck there on that long rough road. When someone died, as part of the funerary practice, the person’s loved ones made the dead person a pair of very good travelling shoes – "Hel-shoes". These shoes were placed on the body so the person could make the long walk in comfort and wouldn’t be tempted to return as a revenant, complaining they couldn’t get to Hel because of poor footwear.
As modern people, we can certainly see the wisdom in not being stuck somewhere we don’t want to be, in particular a place that is neither here nor there. The Norse knew it was best to accept community support, be well prepared and, most of all, to keep walking.

cards.name: Loki
cards.up:
Develop your gifts of oration and clear speech. Play more often – laughter is a gods’-given gift! There may be someone in your life that isn’t what they seem. Try a more light-hearted approach.
Fin, fur,
Scale, skin,
Flight, fight,
Song, sin,
All are available to me.
I shift my shape
And your mind.
I trick my way
Into your play.
Loki is part of that class of gods known as tricksters. Although tricksters taught life lessons by tricking, shape shifting, playing the fool or simply playing, they were not evil. By humbling the righteous and mighty and exposing the unjust, they simple rebalanced what they saw as out of balance.
Loki was a well-equipped trickster! As a shape-shifter, he had few rivals. He was believed to have been able to change into a seal, a woman, a fish, a horse and even a housefly! His children were as varied as Fenrir the wolf and Hel the giantess. Loki played the trickster superbly and is featured in many stories in the mythology of the Norse.
One mythos that displays Loki’s talents is the story of the theft of Thor’s magical hammer, Mjöllnir: Thor awoke one fine morning to find his hammer missing. Little did he know that King Prymr of the Jötnar (giants) had stolen it to blackmail the gods into granting him the hand of the beautiful goddess Freyja. Loki flew around until he came upon Prymr, who engaged him in conversation. Loki acted innocent and soon ascertained that the hammer was buried underground and relayed Prymr’s ultimatum to Thor.
Thor and Loki then visited Freyja and asked whether she would marry Prymr. They got quite the mouthful from her in response! So the gods of Asgard gathered to discuss an alternative strategy. Finally, they decided to cover the burly Thor in a bridal veil and present him to Prymr as Freyja. They hoped that during the wedding proceedings, Thor would get close enough to his hammer to grab it.
And so "Freyja the bride" was presented to Prymr, who happily invited them all to a wedding feast. Thor, the big warrior, began to shovel food through his veil at a great rate, prompting Prymr to question "Freyja’s" massive appetite. Trickster Loki answered, saying "Freyja" had starved herself in her eagerness for the coming nuptials. Unable to control his lust, Prymr peeked behind the veil, only to be met by a set of fiery eyes – definitely not fit for a maiden! Prymr questioned Loki about "Freyja’s" eyes, and Loki responded that her eyes were red because she hadn’t slept for eight nights due to her excitement in meeting him. Finally, when it was time for the ceremony, the Jötnar brought out Mjöllnir and laid it on "Freyja’s" lap to sanctify her prior to the marriage vows. Thor then had his chance and grabbed his hammer and threw off his veil, revealing his true form. Prymr was defeated as were all of his people.
It is wise at this time to take a leaf out of Loki’s book and find a way to laugh at our troubles. There is almost always humour in any situation, and it is a great talent to find it. Should Loki call you, look to the lighter side of the situation. There is one – or at least there is a smarter, brighter alternative.

cards.name: Mani
cards.up:
Time is precious. Be grateful for each passing minute. Using time well is a virtue. Be mindful of how you use your time – which may mean doing very little, if that is of benefit.
A circle
Within a circle,
The whirling wheel.
By nine times three,
I measure my life,
I gather my magic,
I shine my light,
Waiting for Fenrir
To open his jaws.
"Mani" is both one name for the moon as well as the name of a god within the Norse cosmos closely connected with the moon. In the Poetic Edda, it was told that Mani was the brother of the goddess Sol (the sun) and was fathered by Mundilferi (time). It is unusual in any mythos for the moon to have a masculine association. With Mani, we may have the origins of the man in the moon. Both Sol and Mani were seen to circle the earth each day in a chariot.  


Mundilferi is he who begat the moon,
And fathered the flaming sun;
The round of heaven each day, they run,
To tell the time for men.
The Vikings told time by the moon, not the sun. The twenty-eight-day moon cycle was a reliable timekeeper. Also, being seafarers, they were aware of connection between the cycles of the moon and the tides – especially around peak tides of the full moon. Incredibly competent navigators, they relied on the position of the moon, as well as the planets and stars to guide them on their voyages.  


In the Eddic poem "Grimnismal", when Thor asked the dwarf Alvíss about the names for the moon on the other worlds, Alvíss said Mani is called the "moon" by mankind; "the whirling wheel" within Hel; "fiery one" by the gods; "the hastener" by the giants; "the shiner" by the dwarves; and "the counter of years" by the elves. Mani, as a creation of the Aesir (gods) was consumed by the wolf Fenrir at Ragnarok (the end of the world cycle).  


Within the Norse tradition, Mani is a keeper of time and cycles. When we receive this card, we are reminded that time waits for no one and that time is precious. To the Vikings, whose life expectancy was so much shorter than ours, to waste time was to waste life.

cards.name: Odin
cards.up:
Seek guidance to resolve an issue. Gather knowledge from a variety of sources. Respect experience. It takes time to develop wisdom and knowledge – be patient. Spread the runes to receive more knowledge.
The Allfather,
He hangs from the great tree,
Pierced
Between life and death,
Waiting upon the wyrd
To reveal itself,
Patiently.
Wise sacrifice
Serves us,
Honours him.
Odin, who was referred to as the Allfather because of his position as a protector and leader of both gods and humans, was perhaps the most honoured of all Norse gods. He was considered the wisest of all gods, and the most well known of his children is the thunder god Thor.
Odin is a key figure in the Viking mythos. He features in many wonderful stories, most of which have as their theme the pain one must undergo to obtain wisdom. Odin is often depicted with only one eye, as he exchanged the other for a sip of the Well of Wisdom, when he was on his way to the world tree, Yggdrasil. This single sip enabled him to see far, know much and listen to all the stories of the world, which made him wise indeed.
Odin had a subtle duality. He was both a god of bloody war and death and a god of storytelling and intelligence. Warriors honoured him before battle, for they hoped to enter his hall, Valhalla, if they died in combat. Fathers and teachers honoured him, too, in hopes that they would be wise and protective of the children in their care. Those who wished to glimpse their future or gather wisdom through an oracle could use the oracular tool he discovered, the runes, which were symbols most often carved on bone, wood or stone (and are featured in this deck). To obtain the runes from the Well of Wyrd, Odin hung himself from a branch of Yggdrasil, pierced himself with his spear, and peered down into the shadowy waters below, remaining there for nine nights, until the runes revealed themselves to him.
Odin teaches us that education and listening to the wisdom of others is invaluable to own growth and development. The more we know about a situation the better we can assess it, therefore research is rarely wasted. Odin also suggests we consult those with direct experience of topic on which we seek information. If we need guidance in any situation, we can turn to Odin, and he can guide us towards the answers that we need.

cards.name: Ragnarok
cards.up:
Something is coming to an end, only to have something new take its place. We are all subject to the cycle of birth, life, death and rebirth. With death comes an opportunity to start afresh. No matter how difficult the situation, it is not the end of the world.
The wolf,  


Open-mouthed and wild,  


Swallows the sun and the moon.  


The gods turn and die.  


Everything sinks.  


It is gone, we think.  


It is dead, we know.  


And yet, life rises,  


The seeds sprout,  


And light floods the land again.  


Ragnarok is the end stage of the cycle of the Norse mythos. This is where the gods are defeated, the land is destroyed and all life is extinguished. The mighty wolf Fenrir breaks his bonds and swallows the sun and the moon and all things sink into the dark and void as they come to an end.
The cycles of the central Norse mythos – birth, life, death and rebirth, – are reflected both in many traditional stories as well as in the lives of the Norse peoples. Dawn and dusk, light and dark, full moon to dark moon, the cycles of plants and of the births and deaths of the people themselves revealed themselves day after day. In the mythos, the battles between all these extremes play out until, with Ragnarok, the end is played out.
One should not view Ragnarok through the filter of Christianity’s "end of days" scenario, nor as a punishment nor with an end-of-the-world finality. Ragnarok is actually reflective of the cycles of nature and illustrates the idea that everything runs its course, transforms and reforms. After all, the mythos tells us that, after Ragnarok, the gods again begin to rise, light again returns and the cycle begins again.

cards.name: Skadi
cards.up:
Know yourself. It is the most important of life’s work. Express your independence. Let authenticity be your guide. Compromise is part of every relationship, but when compromise pushes you to be someone you are not, a change should be made. There is an easier way to do things. Speak plainly.  


The horizon
Brings me joy.
There is so much to discover.
Unfettered by what is not mine,
I speak my truth, and
I am heard and heeded.
I sing along with my wolves
In harmony. I am myself.
I am Skaði.
Skadi (or Skaði) is a Norse goddess best known in the mountainous parts of the region. Beautiful, strong, resourceful and independent, her name is linked to the words for "unknown" and "darkness" and may even be the source of the word "Scandinavia" – a land dedicated to her. Skadi is a huntress, an archer, a keeper of wolves and, most of all, a lover of snow and of the highest of mountains.  


Her mythos tell us that once married – to a husband she demanded from the other gods as recompense for the death of her beloved father, Þjazi – Skadi tried to live in her new husband’s house. But her husband, Njörðr, was a sea god and lived on an island crashing with waves and smelling of seaweed. The incessant sound of the ocean and screeching of sea birds was too much for Skadi, who was used to the soft silence of the snow and the howling of her wolves. When she spoke of missing her true home and her desire to be independent, she and Njörðr agreed to try alternating homes every nine days. When dividing their time between Nóatún and in Þrymheimr didn’t work out, they decided to live apart, but stay married. Skadi then returned to her beloved mountains, where she hunted from her skis – which she and the god Ull invented!  


The Norse asked Skadi for protection on winter journeys, for success in hunting and for survival in harsh times. When darkness was almost total in the Artic winters, it was she they often referred to. She favoured those who loved the snow and ice and who were honest, open and plain speaking. Her cult extended to the Sámi Arctic region and the Arctic Circle, where people skied for survival, not just for fun.
Should Skadi step into your life with this card, she is reminding you that being honest, direct and respecting your own personal freedom is paramount. If you need to courage to be who you really are, ask Skadi for assistance.

cards.name: Sol
cards.up:
Your sense of personal power will increase. Be confident – your situation will improve quickly. Do not procrastinate. Choose love over hate. Do not be distracted by gossip or mockery – these are lower forms of communication. Surround yourself with positive people.  


Every cell of my being
Reaches up
Like the face of a flower
Turning towards your greatness.
You are the source of all warmth,
The catalyst to my change,
The flow of love to all things,
Golden and beautiful.
I feel filled with now.
I am Sol.
Sol is both a goddess and the sun, itself. Sol and her brother Mani were born of time (Mundilferi) when the universe was being created. Sol was as golden and beautiful as her brother was silvery and light. At first, Sol was not sure of her role within the new world. But then the gods created times of darkness and times of light, assigning Sol the day and Mani night.  


Sol and Mani ride across the sky in horse-drawn chariots. Their steeds are named Árvakr (Early Riser) and Alsviðr (Swift). Other cultures have imagined the sun as a deity riding across the sky on a chariot, too. For instance, the ancient Greeks saw the sun as Helios and his horses. However, most sun deities are seen as male, which makes the female Sol unusual. Perhaps the Norse peoples saw the sun as particularly rare and beautiful, since their lands were dominated by cold, dark and ice. Also, the sun was life giving, as women are givers of life, so they associated the sun with the feminine.  


In some poems, Sol is said to be chased every day by two ravenous wolves, Skoll (Mockery) and Hati (Hate). She manages to outrun them until Ragnarok, when they finally catch and destroy her. This provides an alternative to the mythos of Sol being consumed by the great wolf Fenrir.

cards.name: Sunstone
cards.up:
Trust. Even if a situation seems opaque and unknowable, trust that you will find a way through. Look past the illusion – discover the facts. Seek clarity. Find a different perspective.
White and opaque,
Always sun and no sun.
The stars, they hide
Directionless upon the horizon.
And yet,
There is a way, another way.
By looking through crystal,
Sharply, the stone reveals
Our most desired treasure.
The Vikings’ extraordinary navigational skills led to remarkable raiding and trade successes. Their cultural ambition to greatly extend their territories was supported not only by the solidly built boats they constructed but by their ability to travel the seas with safety and accuracy.  


The Icelandic Sagas of the 1st century AD tell of the Vikings sailing from Bergen, on the coast of Norway, to Iceland, continuing to across to Greenland, and then to a land that is almost certainly Newfoundland. Yet, the Vikings had no compasses (as this incredible navigational feat was realized well before the magnetic compass reached Scandinavia from China), and they were, for the most part, out of sight of land, and thus had little access to navigational land points. Not only that, but the Arctic regions they traversed are notorious for bad weather, including storms and even complete white outs, which meant that neither the sun nor the stars could be relied on for guidance.  


According to Viking records, the secret of this and other navigational feats was the "sólarsteinn" or "sunstone", which was said to reveal the true position of a hidden sun, as occurred in the low contrast days of the almost twenty-four-hour summer days of the extreme north. In the Hrafns Saga it says, The weather was thick and stormy ... The king looked about and saw no blue sky ... then the king took the sunstone and held it up, and then he saw where [the sun] beamed from the stone.  


Modern scientists believe they have solved the mystery. The common Iceland spar, a calcite, changes colour and brightness as it is rotated. Initially, scientists thought the Vikings used such crystals to observe polarisation patterns and in that way pinpointed the direction of the sun. However, research finally proved that by actively depolarizing the light – at what is called the "isotropy point", where the crystal eliminates all polarisation of the light passing through it – it’s possible to glimpse a faint, elongated yellow shape (a phenomenon known as Haidinger’s Brush). This phenomenon gives a one to five-degree indication of the sun’s location – even when there is absolutely no visible sun to measure direction. Genius!  


The sunstone encourages us to trust that there is indeed a way forward, even if we don’t see it initially. By trying different approaches, looking at a situation from different perspectives and using our imagination, we may get where we wish to go.

cards.name: The Nine Worlds
cards.up:
Everything is connected. The fate of one affects the fate of all. Unite for a cause. Darkness and light, good and evil, beginnings and endings, birth and death are all connected. We are never alone.
The mighty ash
Holds all nine,
And the wyrd it flows through
All ends,
All beginnings,
All thoughts.
Each a place for someone:
Sky, earth, trees, ice, fire, death, light.
All united,
All home.
In Norse cosmology, there are nine home worlds (Níu Heimar) or realms, all of which are held within the branches or roots of the world tree, Yggdrasil. In this way, all nine worlds are connected, and each influences the others.
The nine worlds and their inhabitants are as follows:

Ásgarðr (Asgard), home of the Aesir (the gods)

Álfheimr, home of the Ljósálfar (the light elves)

Niðavellir or Svartálfaheimr, home of the dwarves

Miðgarðr (Midgard, Middle-earth), the middle place, home of the humans

Jötunheimr, home of the Jötnar (giants)

Vanaheimr, home of the Vanir (a second group of gods)

Niflheimr, an elemental world of ice and snow

Múspellsheimr, a world of fire and lava, home of the Jötunn Surtr (fire giants)

Hel(heimr), home of the dead and the giantess Hel
The different realms correspond with various aspects of our physical world. For example, Asgard is set in the sky; Hel below ground, where graves might be found; Niflheim is within the ice; and Jotenheim, in forests and wild green places. There are also direct links between worlds, including the rainbow bridge Bifrost that links Asgardhr through Alfheimr to Midgard and allows the gods of Aefir and Vanir to communicate with each other and human beings.
Within the Norse cosmos, we learn that everything is connected. The same tree holds up all nine worlds, different though each world may be, and each world influences the others. While there is a natural ebb and flow, and even battles between elements, the whole ultimately seeks balance and harmony. When all worlds end, at Ragnarok, we know that the cycle begins again and the worlds reform, elements first.

cards.name: The Halls
cards.up:
You will be rewarded for your work. Be brave, even if you are afraid. Now is time to work for the greater good – volunteer.
I am content,
For I have passed from the world
With a sword in my hand,
Blood spilled in your name.
With honour in my heart,
I join the Allfather,
Or is it golden-haired Freyja?
I am carried by the winged women
Screaming my name.
To the Vikings, dying, weapon in hand, fighting to save one’s community was considered the most honourable of deaths. Such warriors were rewarded in the Norse afterlife with admittance to either Freyja’s hall, Sessrúmnir (seat roomer), in Fólkvangr (people’s field) or Odin’s hall, Valhalla, in Asgard.
It was told that Freyja had the first pick of the dead, even above Odin. Those whom Freyja selected were carried to Sessrúmnir by the mighty, winged Valkyries, who served her. Freyja’s chosen dead included brave warriors as well as women who had died an honourable death – either those who fought on the battlefield or those who had committed suicide rather than endure rape or a life of dishonour. Freyja's hall was known as a hospitable and wondrous place, described as "large and beautiful" in the Eddas. Those who joined Freyja were free to do nothing more than practise their fighting skills in preparation for the battle at the end of days at Ragnarok.
Odin’s hall, situated in Asgard, was described in ancient texts as being impressively built, guarded by eagles and wolves and containing long tables groaning with food and mead. Like those chosen by Freyja, the exemplary men that Odin selected to join him in his hall also trained to stand beside Odin at Ragnarok.
Do not confuse these halls with the Christian idea of heaven, though. The halls are not places where spirits lay idle or ready to be reborn. There, life continued in ways the Vikings found ideal – celebrating, fighting and training in happy, purposeful companionship. Admittance to one of the halls was seen as a reward for honour, for courage, for giving up one’s life for the community. The halls remind us to step outside our own needs and consider the greater good.

cards.name: The Norns
cards.up:
While there may be things that are fated, still, our will and energy can alter them. We all receive gifts from the divine at birth, which we can develop or ignore. Focus and energy must be put towards a task if it is to be successful.  


The thread of life shimmers in the dawn.
It is woven by what was;
It is entwined with what is;
And plaited with what will be.
Each has their destiny,
But each, too, their will and magic.
Nothing is certain.
All is in flow.
Yggdrasil, the tree of life that holds the nine worlds within its limbs and roots, grows from the Well of Wyrd. Wyrd is the flow and living force of destiny, which nourishes the world tree and all life. Seated under the tree, ensuring the flow of Wyrd, are the three maiden Norns – Urdr (What was), Verdandi (What is), and Skuld, (What will be).  


These deities weave the destiny of each new baby born. They visit each child and bestow upon them their fate, which they carve in the form of runes into Yggdrasil. While it is tempting to look at the Norns as similar to the Fates in the Greek pantheon, the Norse did not see fate as unalterable, as the Greeks did. Instead, they saw fate as malleable, subject to the will and energy of the individual and the forces of their environment. So while someone could have a destiny carved for them by the Norns, by channelling their own desires and personal energy, they could change it.  


If we turn to mythos, we can see this concept at work: One day, a new baby entered the world to a jarl (Danish chief) and his queen. The Norns travelled to them. The Norns wove and weaved, the silk flying around them, and after a small while, told the mother that her son would be a great warrior, who would attain great glory.
Knowing that such men often died early, the woman begged the Norns, thus: "Please, great women, my son is bound to have an early death should he be a warrior. If this is his only fate, I am both happy and bereft. Whilst warriors keep us safe, their families must suffer, and they must lose their lives! Can you not grant him another talent? Can you not soften his destiny?"  


"Ah", said Urdr, "what we give cannot be taken back."
"But", said Verdandi, "we are not the only influences. We can carve his destiny upon Yggdrasil, but the waters of Wyrd and the magic of the whole can change."
"So", said Skuld, "the will, the wave and the whole shapes his destiny, too."
And so the Norns left the woman and travelled back to the tree of life. They carved the new son’s destiny into its wood, noticing as always that as they did the shape of the fate began to shimmer and move. As always.

cards.name: The Thing
cards.up:
Make a firm decision. Do your due diligence regarding contracts and legal disputes. If you are involved in a political situation at work, get to the heart of the matter – and be flexible. Try diplomacy before resorting to harsher means.
We call upon the gods
To witness and to converse;
To help us be wise, to speak with clarity,
To be just, to be honourable,
To make decisions with eyes fair to the future
That will benefit kin, community and those who
Are yet to walk upon this world.
While Norsemen had a reputation for being savage fighters and raiders, they also had well-established rules for settling disagreements and upholding their laws. All free men (slaves were not included) could attend regional or kinship things, where they would participate in discussions of political and legal issues. In keeping with their oral tradition, all applicable laws and guidelines were recited by a learned speaker. Such speakers were custodians of existing laws and also marked and held new or altered laws.
The arrangement of marriages and the settlement of personal legal disputes were settled at local things. People could also call for an impartial third party to judge a dispute – while some disputes were settled by holmgang (a duel). Depending on the country, things might be ranked from local to regional to national things – like our local, high and supreme courts.
Typically, punishments were not death or torture. The most severe punishments involved the confiscation of land or goods and/or exile. To be thrown out of a kinship group, to lose the support of the community and to be a hated outcast – this was a terrible fate for a Viking.
As most ‘thing sites’ were out in the open, until the last few years (at the time of writing), archaeologists had found very little physical evidence to guide our understanding of the proceedings. However, the 11th century thing site recently discovered beneath a parking lot in the town of Dingwall, Scotland, is just one of a number of new finds. From these, we have learned that things were social as well as legal events. Depending on the size of the thing, marketplaces may have been set up, hunting parties organised to procure food for those attending, and brew masters called from far and wide to provide ale.
Most of us welcome wise counsel when we ask for it and for justice to be served when necessary. Should this card come to your attention, know that you will be granted both those gifts should you be open enough to accept them.

cards.name: Thor
cards.up:
The time for action has come. Hesitate no more. Bust that rut! Protect those weaker than yourself. You can be both forceful and sensitive. You are loved and protected – Thor has his shield arm around you.
The son of the wise
Swings his hammer,
Smashing ignorance and inertia,
Making all new in its force.
Strong is his honour;
Strong are his hands;
Courageous is his heart,
Shielding all in Midgard.
The god Thor, born of the earth goddess Jord and the Allfather Odin, was considered the strongest of the Aesir, the race of Norse immortals. Norse mythology contains many stories of his battles and his bravery – including his struggles with great serpents and his final combat at Ragnarok.
Thor was a god of contrasts. A protector of humans, beloved for his powers over fertility, he was also known for his hot temper. And not only was he a god of action, he was also a poet in a culture that greatly appreciated orators, storytellers, musicians and poets. Yet, as the god of storms, Thor captained a chariot pulled by two savage, giant goats that thundered raucously across the sky.
When Christianity began its spread across the northlands, Thor’s hammer, Mjöllnir, famous for its lethal power, was adopted as a symbol of defiance by those loyal to the old ways. A description of Mjöllnir from the Edda gives us an idea of its power: “… a hammer, which both the frost and the mountain giants know to their cost, when they see it hurled against them in the air, for it has split many a skull of their fathers and kindred. When thrown, it returns to his hand of its own accord.”
Today, we can look to Thor’s energy when we need to take real action. He is a brilliant rut-buster! If you feel inert, tired or frustrated that things are not manifesting, call upon Thor and his mighty hammer to smash a way through. He is protective of his own. You can feel safe knowing that Thor’s might will shield you as you move ahead into the unknown.

cards.name: Valkyries
cards.up:
You can win the battle you face. Let go of your inner restrictions and of others’ expectations. Explore your wild self. Redemption is always available. Be the hero in your own life.
Through the blood and the screaming,
I ride searching.
Sweat, tears, my horse rearing,
I see you.
Brave, dying,
Your hand still upon your sword,
Pain creasing your face.
You see me,
And all changes,
A soft smile of redemption and recognition.
I am Valkyrie!
Some say that near death our whole life flashes before our eyes. But according to the Norse mythology, what flashed before the eyes of Viking warriors as they lay dying upon the battlefield was a beautiful, yet terrible, woman flying on a mighty horse, eyes blazing, singing a song of blood and glory.
The Valkyries were known variously as “choosers of the slain”, “battle maidens”, “mead maidens” and “shield maidens”. They selected the bravest, most worthy of dead warriors – called the einherjar – and spirited them either to Valhalla to spend the afterlife with Odin or to Fólkvangr to reside with Freyja. There, the Valkyries would serve the einherjar mead until they rallied beside the gods for their final battle, Ragnarok.
Some sources suggest Freyja as the mistress of the Valkyries, naming her “Valfreyja”, “mistress of the slain”. Just as the einherjar are considered the foster sons of Odin, the Valkyries are the beloved foster daughters of Freyja. Appropriately, they worked primarily with and under her magic. Freyja also took those women who in life followed her witchcraft most fervently or who were themselves taken in battle to be Valkyries.
Valkyries appeared in the Völsunga saga, in the Eddas and many other places in Norse mythology, and have widely influenced Norse art and music.
For instance, in the Old Norse poem from the Poetic Edda “Helgakviða Hundingsbana I”, we read this:
Then light shone from Logafell,
and from that radiance there came bolts of lightning;
wearing helmets at Himingvani came the Valkyries.
Their byrnies were drenched in blood,
and rays shone from their spears.
And Richard Wagner’s “Ride of the Valkyries”, an excerpt from his opera Die Walküre (The Valkyrie), found popular appreciation after it was used to score a memorable helicopter scene in the movie Apocalypse Now.
Early depictions described the Valkyries as Odin’s ravens – black and terrible, screaming their way across the skies on wild horses and dripping in blood. In later texts, however, they were shown as more beautiful and benevolent, while still retaining their power.
Valkyrie energy is wild, yet offers both redemption and relief from the weariness of battle. Most modern readers do not find themselves in true combat situations, but our lives may still feel like a daily battle. Through their example of power and wildness, they Valkyries urge us to exhibit courage in our daily lives and release ourselves from the bonds of regret.

cards.name: Vegvisir
cards.up:
We are never truly lost – unless we choose to be. We each have a purpose, ‘gods-given’ gifts and direction to fulfil that purpose. Even in the direst of times, know that you are loved and protected. You can find your way, even if the way seems hidden to you.
The storm,
It colours everything
In a rage of blankness and sharp white cold.
It erases what was and is,
And I fear for what will be.
I trace this power,
The lines of meaning,
And I fear my loss no more.
Vegvísir is an Icelandic rune symbol of great power. While scholars are unsure how long magical staves such as vegvísir have been in use – although they have been found on archaeological pieces like stones and weapons from as early as 1400 AD. We first see them officially recorded in manuscripts like the Huld Manuscript, by Geir Vigfusson, in 1860.
The vegvísir is often referred to as the “Viking compass”, not only because it resembles a compass or a sundial, but because of its magical properties, which include protection while travelling through even the most severe storms. It was said that a person possessing the vegvísir would never lose their way, even if the way was not known.
Sigils (symbols used for magical purposes) like vegvísir were painted on objects, worked into talismans and tattooed upon the body – as, for the Vikings, marking oneself with a stave enhanced its power. It is also said those caught in blizzards or sea storms would draw vegvísir on their bodies with their own blood or with charcoal as an emergency measure, believing the sigil would ensure their safety no matter what the elements threw at them.
Even in our contemporary society, the vegvísir is still worn as a tattoo. Most famously, perhaps, Icelandic singer Bjork displays the stave on her left arm. (This author bears a vegvísir tattoo, too!)
Vegvísir assists us in stepping forward into the unknown with confidence. It encourages us to continue our journey, even if the going gets tough. While we may feel lost or directionless, we can take courage in knowing that we will never lose our true path, even if at this moment we don’t know exactly where we are going.

cards.name: Well Of  Wyrd
cards.up:
Magic is real – it is a force in the universe. Your power is real – you are a force in your own life. Do not dwell too long on the past, for you will miss your present and, thus, your opportunity to direct your future. Everything is connected. Even apparently external influences may affect us.
Wyrd flows beneath the great tree
Deeply, roots
Strengthened
With the magic of destiny
I am in flux and in flow.
All circles back
Choice weaves with fate.
The Well of Wyrd (also known as Well of Urd or Well of Urðarbrunnr) is a holy well at the base of the world tree, Yggdrasil. Anything that touches Wyrd’s waters will turn pure white, like the swans that swim upon it. Mentions of the Well of Wyrd are found throughout the Eddas and in particular in the poem “Havamal”, which says that its waters are spread over the roots of the tree by the Norns, who set down laws, they choose lives, for the sons of men, the fates of men.
Connected as they are to the fate-carving Norns, the waters of Wyrd represent the magic of destiny. They flow through Yggdrasil, nourishing and strengthening it. The dew that forms on Yggdrasil’s leaves then drips back into the well, representing a cycle in which the past feeds the present and the future. Since Yggdrasil drips back dew from what has occurred, that dew can circle back and affect the past, which can affect the present, which can affect the future. All is in flux. All circles back.
While all beings receive the blessings and influence of Wyrd, they also have their own life force, which can be used to change the destiny they have been handed. Through this sophisticated, complex approach, the ancient Norse explained how destiny works and even spoke to the nature of time, itself. They have shown us that we always have a choice – even if the Norns have carved us what seems at first to be a difficult destiny.

cards.name: Yggdrasil
cards.up:
You are part of the tree of life. You belong. You are part of something bigger than you realise. You deserve a wonderful life. Your destiny is both fated and shaped by your will. Be present. Be grounded.
I am
Now,
Holding up,
Sending through,
Being with,
Sending forth,
Connected to
Everything.
I am
Life.
Yggdrasil, the tree of life, is the centre of the cosmos. It grows in Asgard, the realm of the gods. It is also known as askr Yggdrasils, which means “the ash tree to which Odin’s (Yggr’s) eight-legged horse, Sleipnir, is tied”.
A mighty ash, Yggdrasil supports within its branches and roots the nine worlds of the Norse cosmos. There, in the various realms, live all beings, including humans and gods. Yggdrasil grows up from the Well of Wyrd, which is the flow and living force of destiny that nourishes both the world tree and life itself. The magic and power that flow through the very heart of the tree travels along its roots and branches to each of the nine worlds. Yggdrasil itself is the home to the three Norns, who carve the fate of all upon the tree, as well as to creatures like dragons, message-carrying squirrels and a great eagle.
Yggdrasil is referred to in many poems in the Eddas. One of the lovelier stanzas, which comes from the Völuspá (“Seeress’s Prophecy,” in the Codex Regius), reads thus:
I know that an ash-tree stands called Yggdrasil,
a high tree, soaked with shining loam.
From there comes the dews, which fall in the valley, ever green.
It stands over the well of fate.
While we are not really expected to believe that there is a literal tree at the heart of the Norse cosmos, this beautiful mythos invites us to view the action of the universe in a way that offers insight into our own lives. Yggdrasil is both central and grounded. It is the symbol of the present, the now, yet it upholds realms and concepts that flow and change. Ancient Yggdrasil is strong and reliable, and it has its own wisdom, as do the most venerable trees in our modern world.

cards.name: Ceridwen
cards.up:
The Initiator
In the old Welsh story of the enchantress Ceridwen, she chases Gwion Bach, a young boy who has consumed three drops of potion from her cauldron of inspiration – a potion which she herself brewed and which she intended for her son. Her long pursuit of the boy makes it possible for him to discover and draw on the new knowledge that he’s acquired in order to shape-shift, to try to escape her. But the dark goddess cannot be eluded; finally, after submitting him to tests of his newly acquired prowess, Ceridwen catches Gwion Bach, swallows him up, and rebirths him as Taliesin, who became the greatest of all prophets and bards.
The story of Ceridwen presents the cauldron as a symbolic womb: the source of rebirth and transformation. She’s the keeper of the cauldron, and her story reflects the role of women in our native mythologies as the source of life and creative power. To drink from Ceridwen’s cauldron of inspiration, then, is an initiation: the beginning of a long and difficult rite of passage, and of the metamorphoses which inevitably must follow.
Ceridwen reminds us that as a consequence of even the most challenging initiations, there’s the possibility of great renewal. Have courage: drink from the cauldron of inspiration, even if you don’t quite believe that the potion is meant for you – and even if you don’t yet know the nature of the transformations it will require of you.

cards.name: Shape-Shifting
cards.up:
To shape-shift reflects an unbearable lightness of being, the antithesis to rigidity, and European myth and tradition is overflowing with shape-shifting women. Goddesses shift constantly between human and animal form; men marry seal-women, and fairy-tale heroines transform the bears who are their husbands back into men.
These traditions reflect an ancient worldview in which humans were seen as an intrinsic part of the natural world and were related to the other-than-humans who inhabit it alongside us – rather than being separate from nature and possessing dominion over all the other creatures within it, as we imagine ourselves to be today. These shape-shifting beings represent a rich and necessary wildness within us that modern civilization has all but wiped out.
To shape-shift is to embrace transformation in all its unexpected complexities. It's also to acknowledge the fluid relationship between human and animal, and to respect and cultivate the wisdom and ways of being of other-than-humans. By imagining ourselves as one with our animal relatives, we can come to see that there are other ways of imagining the world and our place in it. We can discover ways of living more intensely, more richly, and with a deeper sense of belonging to this multilayered and animate world.

cards.name: The Morrigan
cards.up:
Death and Rebirth
The Morrígan is a complex goddess in Irish myth who was primarily associated with the cycle of death and rebirth. In one old poem, she was referred to as the 'phantom queen,' or the 'terror of the night'. She was associated with war, too: not only as a symbol of imminent death but also to influence the outcome of battles. In this context, she's another manifestation of the Sovereignty goddess, guarding a territory and its people and providing them with military aid, or protection for the king.
The Morrígan, with her many faces, encourages us to reclaim the Dark Feminine, embracing the dark as well as the light. Most of us have grown up in a world where women can so often be demonized: the wicked witch, the bad mother, the madwoman... But in these encounters with the Dark Feminine which are provided by the over-culture, we rarely see her other faces, and her more positive qualities: those of transformation, healing, and rebirth. This does women a great disservice, leaving us disconnected from the full range of possibilities for the Divine Feminine.
The Dark Feminine is a part of us; we find her in the deepest and oldest parts of our psyche. She expresses the very necessary energy that captures the mysteries of womanhood and magic, the chaos of creation and destruction, of birth and death and rebirth, of rage and righteous wrath, of fierce compassion, sexuality, and spiritual and physical ecstasy.

cards.name: Sovereignty
cards.up:
The Power of the Land
Celtic mythology is highly goddess-centered: the creative essence of the universe was female, and women represented the spiritual axis of the world. But above all, the Celtic Divine Female in her various incarnations was deeply grounded and rooted in place, indivisible from her distinctive landscapes. They are manifestations of Sovereignty, a quality of the goddess of the land who was its guardian and protector. Sovereignty was the spirit of the Earth itself, the anima mundi, a deeply ecological force.
The power of Sovereignty was paramount. During the reign of a king favored by the goddess, the land was fertile and prosperous, and the tribe was victorious in war. But if the power she bestowed was abused, then the people invited disaster.

Sovereignty is an ally who reminds us that the land must be respected. While there's mutual respect between the goddess and the king, the land and the people, nature and culture, feminine and masculine, then life is filled with abundance. But when we refuse to live in balance and fall out of harmony with the world around us, the fertile land becomes the Wasteland. In this context, Sovereignty also reminds us that the source of our power as women – and the image of the Divine which lives within each of us – comes from the land. We must now become its guardians and protectors.

cards.name: Cailleach
cards.up:
Protector of the Wild
In Irish and Scottish folklore, the Cailleach (pronounced ‘Kalyack’) is the divine hag, the creator-goddess of the land who gives shape to the Earth throughout all its long ages. Stories tell of how she constructed enormous mounds and megaliths in a single night, and of how she shaped the hills and the mountains and caused great lakes to form.
Like the cycles and seasons of the natural world over which she presides, the Cailleach renews herself constantly: each year in spring, or every hundred years, and usually by bathing in a certain body of water. But above all, the Cailleach is presented as the fierce protector of the Earth and the guardian of its balance. She ensured that humans could not take more than the land could give. Hunters had a great respect for her and, if they followed her instructions on which deer to cull and when, she ensured that they were always provided with enough food and pelts.
In these troubled times and challenging environmental conditions, we women need to embrace our inner Cailleach: to stand up for the integrity and health of the wild places and creatures of this world. The Cailleach is our ally in this work, teaching us that we are the land, and the land is us; and reminding us also that to grow into an Elder is to become strong, as enduring as the beautiful old bones of this Earth.

cards.name: Bean Si
cards.up:
The Keening Woman
The Bean Sí ('banshee') in Irish folklore is an Elder female spirit who heralds the death of members of certain old families she's associated with, usually by screaming, wailing, shrieking, or keening. Her hair is wild, and her eyes are red and raw from constant weeping.
The Bean Sí is associated with the Bean Chaointe – the keening woman – who traditionally led the mourning of the dead by performing a kind of funeral lament at wakes. In this way, she acted as a midwife of sorts, but one who facilitated the passage through death, rather than birth. It was believed that she functioned as a kind of psychopomp: a soul guide.
The act of keening is an act of catharsis. It's also about honoring our grief – grief for our own hurts, the hurts of loved ones, and the hurts of the world. Grieving is a normal and necessary response to pain and loss. The Bean Sí tells us that we must allow ourselves the time and space to grieve for the dead, and for the dead parts of us that we need to leave behind in order to make progress along our Journey.

cards.name: The Fisher Kings Court
cards.up:
Otherworldly Treasures
The Fisher King's Court, in the large body of European legends about the quest for the Grail, is an Otherworldly source of nourishment and treasure which can sometimes be seen in this world. But this magical place, which is usually situated on the banks of a great, wide river, offers us more than just fine food and jewels: it's the source of all the treasures of the living Earth. The wild things; the beauty of the natural world.
In European traditions, the Otherworld is a lush and fertile place. It might sometimes be dangerous, with ample traps for the proud or unwary, but it's usually envisaged as a land of abundance. It's a place of beauty and harmony, not of darkness and terror. A country which exists outside the laws of time and space, it's home to deities, spirits, and supernatural beings – and to our ancestors. It's a world which runs parallel to our own, and which might sometimes seep into it.
The Otherworld is elusive, accessible only at certain times of the year, at certain 'thin' or threshold places, or by invitation. For our ancestors, it was just as real as our own world; it was simply perceived in different ways – not with the physical senses but with what we might think of as the psychospiritual senses. This card reminds us that we'll always find our greatest source of joy and nourishment in the magic of the land, which is the gift of the Otherworld. It reminds us to be grateful for, and respectful of, the abundance we're offered.

cards.name: The Isle Of Women
cards.up:
Women's Mysteries
In Irish mythology, Tír na mBan, the Isle of Women, is an island which lies far across the western sea. Sometimes called the 'land of the living,' it's a beautiful country of many colors, filled with music, flowers, trees, and birds. In the British tradition, Avalon, too, is an Isle of Women whose inhabitants – epitomized by the character of Morgan le Fay – are healers and scholars.
The Isle of Women is a place in which women's mysteries are celebrated; a place which allows them to be explored in safety and sisterhood. It's a hidden and protected land; men come here uninvited at their peril. The women's mysteries which are honored and explored here include the blood mysteries of menarche, menstruation, motherhood, and menopause: the creative mysteries which spark the blossoming of new life, art, and ideas.
The archetypal feminine, in all its forms, is also celebrated on the Isle of Women. It's a place where the lost or damaged feminine can be explored, reclaimed, and reimagined. It's a temenos, a sanctuary. It's protected from the outer world, and what's contained within it belongs only to women. This card invites you to find a safe place, and to rest a while as you explore the mysteries of the feminine. In this sacred, inviolable space, you can explore the manifold ways in which those forces show up in your own life.

cards.name: The Crossroads
cards.up:
In European mythology, the crossroads is a liminal place, and one where gods and Otherworldly beings might linger. It's a site where sacred encounters take place: with friends, strangers, and perhaps with beings from outside of our reality. You might encounter your ancestors there. Approach it in a spirit of both reverence and caution.
To arrive at the crossroads is to arrive at a choice point. You might hesitate and hover on it for a while, but you cannot stay there forever; eventually, you'll be forced to make a decision. As a consequence of the path you choose to take here, your life will be forever changed. But the path you should take is rarely obvious, and the events that might follow from your choice are often unpredictable.
The Crossroads card, then, represents a place where you're not in control. But if change is both inevitable and undiscoverable, don't fear it: listen to whoever you might encounter there, and then trust yourself to make the choice. Because there are no wrong choices at the crossroads; every path holds out the promise of a homecoming. And wherever you might find yourself traveling, you'll learn something important and necessary from the experience.

cards.name: Well
cards.up:
The Source of Life
Wells, in the native traditions of Britain and Ireland, have their roots in the Otherworld; they are gateways between worlds. The water which flows from them offers up Otherworldy nourishment – not just physical, but spiritual. Because of that, wells were recognized as sacred, just as they have been by nearly every culture on the planet, and throughout every age. These wells and springs which originated in the Otherworld would once have been dedicated to Sovereignty, the goddess of the land who bestowed the gifts of the Otherworld.
The gifts of the wells are many. Some were known for their healing powers; others for granting fertility. Magical fish which lived in the wells – salmon, or sometimes trout – might appear to those who would come seeking insight and foreknowledge. These fish are credited as granters of imbas, a form of intuitive knowledge and wisdom which is the Otherworld’s greatest gift.
The water of the well, then, is the source of life and spiritual wisdom. But the Source of Life must be cared for; a good well must be tended. If you neglect a well, you’re also neglecting the soul of the land; you’re neglecting your own soul and what nourishes it. The Well card invites you to replenish and renew yourself in the freely given waters of life – but it also asks you to respect and treasure their source. In the spirit of reciprocity, we offer in return our love, and our gratitude for all in this world that upholds us.

cards.name: The Grail Bearer
cards.up:
Spiritual Nourishment
Although the medieval Grail legends are usually presented as centered around a heroic quest, women are central to Grail mythology: they're the bearers of the Grail, and its messengers.
Like all the cups and cauldrons in the old Celtic texts and stories, what's contained in the Grail, and offered by the Grail Bearer, is the creative, generative essence of the Otherworld, which animates the land. And so the quest for the Grail, the giver and sustainer of life, is a quest to respect and restore the anima mundi, the soul of the world.
The Grail Bearer card reminds us that all life is sacred, and that all life is a precious gift. We didn't come to this world to be alone, but to be a part of a community of humans and other-than-humans, fully entangled in the web of life on this beautiful, animate Earth. All of this life that we're a part of wants to be in relationship with us. If only we can learn how to listen and to see, we can come to understand that every bird wants to sing to us, and every flower to open for us. The Grail Bearer encourages us to understand that we're a part of an animate world, to feel the sacred heartbeat of life all around us – which nourishes us and supports us, if only we choose to let it in.

cards.name: River
cards.up:
Flow
Rivers and springs, the old stories tell us, have their origins in the Otherworld and carry with them its life-giving nourishment. In European myth and folklore, they're closely identified with divine women who are present in the water's flow.
From the perspective of a map, the path of a river might seem to be fixed – but the truth is that they're dynamic beings. A river's course will shift and flex during its long lifetime, and its waters will swell or diminish from day to day. Sometimes, a river will rise and break free of its banks, casting off all that restrains its inexorable flow. It's the ultimate in flexibility, but its strength must not be underestimated: when rock meets water, it's rock that always eventually gives way.
A river is a silver thread, snaking through the land. She's everywhere and nowhere; she travels on past us, but still she remains. She's the flow of all our longings, the flow of inspiration that propels us through this life. She knows exactly where she's headed – from the very beginning, she's always on her way home to the sea. The river always leads you home, if you can only bring yourself to trust the flow of life as it carries you onward.
This card invites you to trust that flow of life; to stop resisting and believe that the course you're taking – though often it will twist, and sometimes it will turn back on itself – will eventually lead you home.

cards.name: Selkie
cards.up:
The Soulskin
The Selkie’s story tells of a woman whose sealskin has been stolen by the man who wants her to stay with him and be his wife. Because of that theft, she’s forced to remain in the human form which Selkies are usually able to adopt just once a month, at the time of the Full Moon. As a result, the seal-woman is quite literally taken out of her briny element and trapped on the land, where she cannot find a way to fully belong. She loses her place in the world, and consequently loses her story: her sense of who she really is, her authentic self.
The Selkie, then, represents yearning – yearning for a part of ourselves that we feel we’ve lost, or maybe a part that we feel we might once have had but never really understood. So many of us lose our skins, and we lose them young. The consequences of this loss, of this disconnectedness, this separation from our true nature and what nourishes and empowers us, often becomes apparent only after many years.
This card encourages you to remember your lost skin – your unique sense of self, your unique creative power as a woman. To remember the pelt that once smelt so wonderfully of home and of yourself, in all your natural wildness. How can you begin to grow a new skin – a skin that represents the heart of who you are now, and allows you to accept and fully embody the Wild Woman within?

cards.name: Elen
cards.up:
Pathmaker and Guide
In an old Welsh story called ‘The Dream of Macsen Wledig’, Elen, an Otherworldly princess of Britain, appears to the Roman emperor Macsen in an aisling: a dream-vision. She acts as a guide, captivating him with a vision of a beautiful land across the waters, and a beautiful woman there with whom he instantly falls in love. And so Elen reels Macsen in along the thread of her dream-paths, bringing him to her so that he can marry her and serve the land alongside her as its king.
The story tells us that it was Elen who built the so-called Roman roads which joined up, for the first time, the various remote regions of the land. The story firmly states that the men of Britain would have allowed the roads to be built for no one but her, because she was ‘native to the land’; the land’s representative. Elen, like so many other female characters in Celtic myth and story, is a representative of Sovereignty, the goddess of the land.
The building of these great connecting roads is the reason why Elen has now come to be known as Elen of the Ways. Elen, then, can be seen as an ally on our journey, a native goddess and guide who helps us to dream into being our own unique pathway through life. Look for her in your dreams.

cards.name: Well Maiden
cards.up:
The Voice of the Otherworld
There's an old story among the Grail legends which tells that once, maidens would emerge from wells throughout the land to offer food and drink to any traveler who came by and was in need of it. The Well Maidens' power came from the Otherworld, and it was the source of life for the land. When a king who didn't respect the old ways raped a Well Maiden, they withdrew back into the wells. As a consequence, the land became a Wasteland, and the story tells us, the Voices of the Wells were lost. The link between our world and the Otherworld was broken, the land lost its heart, and we lost the bridge – the Divine Feminine – which connected us to it.
The Well Maiden is a living bridge between the Otherworld and our own; she's a conduit for the wisdom of the Otherworld and mediates its life-giving force. As an ally on our Journey, she invites us to re-weave that connection: to remember the time when people and the land were one, when the wisdom of the Otherworld could more easily be accessed. She reminds us that we need to reclaim and honor the Divine Feminine; to integrate into ourselves the feminine mystery which has been suppressed over countless centuries. Only then can we restore the balance which will lead us out of the Wasteland; only then will the Voices of the Wells be heard again.

cards.name: Island
cards.up:
Boundedness and Isolation
An island can represent many ways of being in the world. It can be a source of safety and security, or it can represent exile and isolation. Sometimes, it can represent both. Sometimes, in order to feel safe, we exile ourselves from the things we formerly knew and loved. We separate from the world and make of ourselves an island. Sometimes this is a positive thing – a necessary withdrawal to lick our wounds and gain respite. Sometimes the withdrawal is in some way forced upon us – perhaps because we can’t accommodate the world as we know it or feel ourselves fully a part of it.
All edges are transitional places, and the greatest edges of all are the places where land meets sea. These edges might seem gentle on a still summer’s day when the sun warms the shallows and the soft sand cradles you, but to inhabit an island, you must also be able to face the storm.
Its edges might seem to define an island on a map, but from the island’s perspective, its edges aren’t always strictly defined. They shift with weather and with the tides, in a never-ending dance between land and sea. Like the sea on an island beach, we too ebb and flow; we soften sometimes, allow ourselves to seep into another ecosystem, then retreat into the safety of our own world. This card reminds us to ponder that mystery, and never to resist its natural flow.

cards.name: Sea
cards.up:
Plumbing the Depths
The sea is so changeable that it's impossible to really anticipate its moods. The sea is continuously in motion, ebbing and flowing, shifting from tide to tide. On a stormy day it's intimidating, a reminder of the raw, unpredictable power of this beautiful, animate Earth we inhabit. On a bright summer's day when the sun warms the shallows and the light sparkling off the water lifts our spirits, we might remember that it's the home from which we originally came.
Whatever face it might turn to us, the essence of the sea is the depth of its waters. This card encourages us to go deep, even if we're afraid there might be monsters. There are times when we need to step out of the shallows of life and plumb the depths – to turn inward and find the source of wisdom that lies deep inside us. To make that choice, we need courage. Inside each of us there's a vast and deep terrain, and to begin to understand who we really are, what our gifts are, and what we might dream of becoming in this life, we need to begin to explore it.
We need to move out of the safe shallows of the ego and our conscious mind and turn our attention to all that remains hidden within us and is unconscious. Dreams are one of the most important ways that our unconscious psyche can communicate with us, and so the Sea card invites us above all to pay attention to our dreams, to the images and characters and scenarios which present themselves to us while we're sleeping.

cards.name: Pilgrimage
cards.up:
The pilgrim's journey is always spiritual in nature. It's undertaken in order to have a revelation of some kind, or to find some deeper understanding of the world and our place in it. A pilgrimage asks that we give up everything so we might learn what is truly ours to keep. It's a search for knowledge, a search for becoming. And a pilgrimage begins also with a longing: a longing for deep connection, for true, nurturing community, or simply for change.
A pilgrimage, above all, asks us to surrender to the Journey and open ourselves up to new ways of traveling and seeing. The pilgrim's path is designed to wind its way across unknown and often rough territory, and the long, arduous Journey requires endurance, resilience, and focus. But there's nothing for it but to keep walking. Step by bumpy step; one foot in front of the other. The path will fade behind you, and there will be no way back. And once you understand just how far you must travel, it can be hard to confront the long, challenging road ahead.
That's why we must look for, and be able to welcome, the help of allies along the way. The most valuable allies are those who teach us that we cannot succeed alone – and more, that it's meaningless to succeed alone, for an essential feature of the Heroine's Journey is uncovering the joys of and necessity for community. Pilgrim paths are peopled by many others, and if we're open, we'll find many kinds of allies along the way. Only some of them are human.

cards.name: The Return
cards.up:
When the Heroine returns from her Journey, she brings back to the world a gift – a way of seeing, of being – which is uniquely hers. She must begin to decide how, using those unique gifts, she can work to restore the fertile feminine principle to the world, to speak for the Earth itself, and so take responsibility for the healing of this Wasteland.
