In the challenged world we live in, our newfound wisdom should above all be grounded, rooted, and earthy: the creative, regenerative power of life which comes from an understanding of our place in the wider web of life on this Earth. Our task on our return is to help bring about a re-enchantment of our relationship with the Earth.
But it's not always easy to return, and sometimes we might want to refuse it. Sometimes it's easier by far to sink into the magical Otherworldliness of the Journey, and for some of us there's a strong temptation to stay withdrawn from a challenging everyday world, to go into permanent retreat, or to make the search for personal enlightenment and self-illumination our lifetime's work. But if we do, chances are that, sooner or later, the world will come knocking. Because, as the world (and our own species) lurches from crisis to crisis, as we listen to the cry of a grieving Earth, the call to return is strong.
The Return card invites us to imagine a place in which we can be grounded, rooted; a place in which our particular gifts and wisdom can flourish; a place in which we can fully embrace the natural world around us, and our part in it. A place from which we can speak.

cards.name: Reclaiming The Feminine
cards.up:
A core task in a woman's Journey through life is to discover and then integrate the feminine principle which has been repressed over countless centuries. It's an antidote to the masculine principle whose qualities have dominated our cultural discourse here in the West for far too long. We need the feminine to balance out that dogged drive for success and progress, and devotion to intellectual, rational, and goal-oriented traits.
Feminine qualities of relatedness enable us to appreciate and live in harmony with other humans, as well as the other-than-humans who share the planet with us. They enable us to appreciate the rhythms of the natural world, as well as the rhythms of our physical body and the cycles and seasons of our lives. These qualities of the feminine principle
also include the instinctive, feeling qualities traditionally associated with the heart and the soul.
But reclaiming the feminine isn't just about embracing all the things which make us feel good: we need to encounter the Dark Feminine too. This isn't necessarily the 'negative' aspect of the feminine; rather, it's the expression of the very necessary creative and chaotic energy which allows us to experience the full range of women's mysteries.
This card invites us to delve deep to uncover our inner source of female wisdom and to embrace our own unique creativity and life-giving qualities, in the spirit of both our own growth and our service to the world.

cards.name: Cave
cards.up:
Incubation
Throughout Europe, our ancestors descended into caves to listen to the whisperings of the Otherworld. It was believed that the Otherworld would grant prophetic visions to those who came to caves, and so many ancient oracles were located in them. Seers, shamans, poets, and other intermediaries between humans and the Divine would practice prolonged isolation in caves in their search for knowledge and illumination. Such visions could be received from ancestors as well as from the gods.
Initiatory rituals often took place in caves; they were key to the Eleusinian, Dionysian, Orphic, and Mithraic mystery traditions of ancient Greece and Rome. Caves are dark and womb-like, and the passages which lead to them reflect the process of birth – the journey out of the safety of the womb and into an uncertain world. The entry passages are also characteristic of near-death experiences. The cave, then, is a portal to new life.
The rebirth which begins to be dreamed into being in the cave is at the heart of the Heroine's Journey. The Cave card, then, invites us to shut ourselves away for a while from the clamor of the outside world. Held safely in the soft and healing darkness, we can begin to reimagine ourselves. Here in the cave is where our transformation begins – a profound and lasting transformation which can only emerge from time spent in the darkest of places.

cards.name: The Buried Moon
cards.up:
The Hidden Feminine
In a very old tale from the fens of eastern England, the Moon decides to take a journey into the marshland and becomes trapped there by the ‘dark things’ which inhabit it. She’s buried in a black hole because the dark things are intent on destroying the power of the Moon; they despise her light and want to extinguish it.
The Buried Moon card represents the lost heart of the feminine: the heart which holds all the secrets of sustaining life. Hers is a story that countless women have experienced through all the long ages of our existence in patriarchal cultures which are so afraid of female power that they’ve gone to extravagant lengths to suppress it, creating new stories to cover it up. The witch-hunters who long ago buried the Moon.
But like the light of the Moon, which still escapes through a slit between the stone that covers her and the marshy land that encloses her, our light can also shine through any cracks we can pry open. The light of those feminine qualities which have been buried so deeply inside us that we’ve forgotten they even exist, let alone where to find them.
So, at this stage of our Journey, the Moon is an ally who encourages us to go deeply back inside ourselves and search for the feminine mystery which has been suppressed over countless centuries: women’s ways of knowing and being, constantly waxing and waning and associated not just with the menstrual cycles of the female body, and therefore with motherhood, but with the wider sphere of death and rebirth.

cards.name: Medow
cards.up:
Flourishing and Regenerating
A meadow sings to us of summer: of sensuality, of exuberance, of life in the fullness of its most abundant flow. When we look at a meadow, we can clearly perceive the greening of life – what the medieval German mystic Hildegard of Bingen called viriditas: the Divine force which she believed animates and nourishes the world, and in which all living things participate. A meadow opens its arms wide to the skies – although so many living things can shelter and hide among its long grasses and bushy wildflowers.
Beneath the surface of a meadow lies a rich tapestry of roots, as different species intermingle and weave themselves together into a beautiful, diverse whole. The Meadow card, then, reminds us that the Heroine's Journey is at heart about serving the community as well as ourselves. We can only flourish together; there's little to nourish the world in a monoculture or a single-species lawn. The grasses and wildflowers in a meadow are planted in rich soil that teems with life – a medium in which their seeds will germinate and bloom for the good of all who inhabit it. A meadow can shelter, nourish, and feed so many different species.
This card asks us to remember that women are so full of gifts; we're containers for so much life. We're a critical element in the abundance of this beautiful, animate Earth. We were made to flourish, and we deserve to flourish. It's our birthright, our heritage, and the driving force of this Heroine's Journey that we're on.

cards.name: Initiation
cards.up:
Initiation is a necessary precursor to deep transformation. If we think of transformation as an alchemical process, then the first stage of alchemy is the initiatory stage; ancient alchemists called it the nigredo ('blackening'). This word reflects the 'dark night of the soul' that we pass through when we're enduring deep and rending changes in our lives.
The nigredo is the longest and most difficult phase in alchemy, during which the substance that's transforming suffers deeply. The goal during this initial phase of transformation is to reduce the individual to her bare essence, to strip her down to her most essential parts. Alchemists called this work mortification: literally, 'facing the dead parts.'
The next stage of this initiatory process – called the albedo ('whitening') – represents the psychospiritual purification that results from our suffering during the nigredo. And all major initiations are containers for meaning in this way. They're invitations not just to learn, but to finally grow into ourselves – to let the dead wood fall and more fully reveal the thriving, living heart of who we are. The Initiation card reminds you that if you can brace yourself for a rocky ride and surrender to the Journey, nothing will ever be the same again.

cards.name: Mountain
cards.up:
Vision and Inspiration
Mountains lend texture and shape to our landscapes and form boundaries between communities and countries. They create weather, influence the flow of bodies of water, and reflect the strength and endurance of the land through all the long ages of the Earth.
Mountains are formed as a consequence of profound upheavals: when pieces of the Earth's crust collide, when molten rock from deep inside the Earth erupts through the crust and piles up on itself, and when stresses in tectonic plates cause cracking and faulting of the planet's surface. Over the course of many millions of years, wind, rain, ice, and gravity have gradually worn down the surface of the mountains, creating the unique shapes and personalities that they possess today.
It's not surprising, then, that mountains should inspire awe; that we should think of them not only as refuges but as sacred places. The mountain is the place we turn to for vision and inspiration – but it's not always an easy ride. After the inevitable difficult ascent, we might become dizzy as we look down from the heights. We might fear the extremity, we might fear being pushed to or beyond our limits. But if we can only hold strong, the reward for our effort is an ability to see clearly, and to understand how we might dream our visions into being. This card encourages us to persevere, and to dream dreams that are as large and wide as we need them to be.

cards.name: Rooted
cards.up:
​This card signifies the aim of the Journey we're exploring in this oracle. It reminds us that the day of the heroic quest – with its all-conquering, dragon-slaying Hero saving the world one sword-stroke at a time – is over. The notion of the Hero's Journey is derived from the intensely individualistic, human-centric Western cultural mythology that for centuries has had us firmly in its grip. But the Journey that women need now is a Post-Heroic Journey, a Heroine's Journey, a path to understanding how deeply enmeshed we are in the web of life on this planet.
​This Journey leads us back to a sense of our own grounded belonging to this Earth and asks us what we have to offer it. To be rooted, then, is to become native to our places again, to ground ourselves solidly in the land where we live and the stories and traditions of our native and ancestral places.
​
​To be rooted is not to stand still, or to imagine that we now have all the answers to the mystery of our lives in this challenged and changing world. Rather, it's to recognize that the purpose of life is growth and transformation, and that the Journey never ends. Spring comes, and the planted seed heaves itself out of the fertile, dark soil and starts to grow. In summer, it flowers and flourishes, and in autumn it reaps its harvest. In winter, it rests and replenishes its roots. And then it's time to circle back to the beginning and set off down the road once more

cards.name: The Call
cards.up:
The Heroine's Journey always begins with a call to change. Sooner or later, we're called to wake up. It's a call to rise up out of the unendurable everyday and inhabit a full, authentic life. And when we hear it, we must answer this call, or forever be lost in the Wasteland.
The call can come at many different times. When we find ourselves unhappy in our jobs, in our marriages. When we develop chronic illnesses, anxiety, or other mental health issues. When rage or grief threaten to overwhelm us. When we begin to contemplate our own mortality, to question who we are, who we might have been, who we might yet become. When, for the first time, we finally see the Wasteland for what it is.
The call comes when we break. It comes to us sooner or later, but it comes. And whenever it happens, we know there's a Journey we must undertake. Something deep inside us knows that there's somewhere we should be going. And so, in the end, no matter how long or hard we resist it, and whether or not we think we can, we go because we must. We go, because to stay is to die.

cards.name: Cairn
cards.up:
Portal to the Mystery
At some point – or indeed, at many points – along the Journey of our lives, we'll find ourselves experiencing a sense of awe or 'otherness' which seems to arise from some inner necessity burning brightly at our core. If we're willing to apprentice ourselves to these teachers, we begin to find ourselves consumed by questions about the ultimate truth and meaning of our existence. But these are not questions which have easy answers; perhaps the heart of the answer lies in pondering the question. The mystery of life and our place in it is something to sit with, not to solve.
Mystery is unknowable to the rational mind. To be comfortable in the company of mystery is to be willing to penetrate the deep shadows of the cairn – to take a walk into the dark and sit with it for a while. Mystery relieves us of the fiction that we know exactly where we're going, and that we're the sole authors of the story we're living. It keeps us on our toes.
When we embrace mystery, the world declares itself to be a place of potentialities, and our Journey through it becomes a journey of discovery. The Cairn card proposes that we give up our need for control. Surrender to the mystery, it whispers, and the light which is designed to lead you out of the dark places will always be able to find you.

cards.name: Rhiannon
cards.up:
The Story Carrier
In the old Welsh text The Mabinogion, Rhiannon, another representative of the goddess Sovereignty, rides out of the Otherworld on a white horse to take Dyfed’s king, Pwyll, as her husband. She’s feisty and resourceful, and at first, she sets the pace in their relationship and seems to hold all the power. But Rhiannon is distrusted by the people of Dyfed, betrayed by her own women, and doubted by her husband. She’s wrongly accused of killing and eating her own son, and her penance is to tell the false story of her great sin to all who come to Dyfed’s court. Eventually, her son is found, and her own true story can emerge.
Like Rhiannon, we must remember and uphold our own truths as we progress along our Heroine’s Journey; we must always insist on telling our own stories, ourselves. These stories emerge directly from our own authentic, lived experience. During the course of a lifetime, each of us will encounter stories that are told about us and against us by others, and some of them will become so deeply interwoven into the fabric of our everyday lives that unpicking them can be hard.
Rhiannon, then, is an ally who helps us to discern, and uphold, the stories about our lives which we believe to be true. The stories which come from our own beautiful hearts, and from ways of being and enduring that are unique to us alone.

cards.name: Lake
cards.up:
What Lurks Beneath
In European myth and folklore, lakes are mysterious, magical, and sometimes ominous places. In Welsh mythology, for example, the gateway to Annwn – the Welsh name for the Otherworld – could often be found at the bottom of deep lakes. In the Gaelic traditions of Scotland and Ireland, lakes could harbor monsters such as the each uisge – the water horse – who would steal away an unsuspecting maiden and carry her to his home at the bottom of the lake to be his wife.
The ancient Greek philosopher Socrates exhorted us to 'know thyself,' and in that spirit the Lake card invites us to confront our own monsters and to explore our Shadow side. According to Carl Jung, the Shadow archetype isn't necessarily the 'dark side' of us; rather, it represents all the personal traits we've ignored, denied, or cut off from our
awareness in order to create what we imagine to be a functioning personality. In working with the Shadow, our aim should not be to suppress or repress any aspect of who we are, but to come to know all sides of ourselves.
To integrate the Shadow is to confront our inner demons and acknowledge the darkness within us – because being conscious of this is the only way to understand, and deal with, our destructive tendencies. This work, then, involves the inner strength and commitment to be able to question our core beliefs and values. But the rewards are great – in coming to understand who we really are, we can make significant progress along our Heroine's Journey, and move into a new, authentic, and meaningful stage of life.

cards.name: The Fall
cards.up:
When we heed the Call to change and step off the Threshold, imagining that we're going to set our feet firmly on the new road ahead of us, we might instead find ourselves stumbling, missing the path, and plummeting down into the dark.
Let yourself fall. Sometimes we have to let ourselves fall in order to kickstart the process of transformation to which we've now committed ourselves. We have to let go of old ways of thinking, of old limits, to let the old ways die to make room for the new. Because once you've stepped across that threshold, it is for sure a severance, a kind of death: you can never go back to what you were before.
There's no question that it's hard to fall forward into the wind, to let yourself topple off the edge of all that's known and familiar – even if that old life isn't serving you. It's a big step, this first movement
toward wholeness.
 It means leaving behind the safety of familiar social structures and supports. It's a massive letting go. But these are edge-dwelling days, and if we want to live up to them, we must stand there consciously, aware of the troubled times and the endangered planet, and then of our own volition step out across this first threshold. And at some point during the fall, you might find that you're flying, after all.

cards.name: Old Woman Of Dreams
cards.up:
The Maker of Visions

An old Scottish folktale tells of an old woman and an old man who live in a cave high up in the Cuillin mountains on the Isle of Skye. The couple are the creators of all the dreams of the world. The Old Woman of Dreams has deep vision. She can see and understand everything that’s happening in the world by looking into a dark pool in the cave. She uses this knowledge to create the substance out of which her husband crafts the dreams of the world – the two of them together quite literally dreaming the world into being.

The story tells us of a young girl who loses her way in misty weather and stays with the couple for a year and a day, helping them with their work. As a consequence, the girl comes to understand the importance of apprenticeship. She emerges from the old woman’s tuition with the knowledge of how to interpret dreams: a skill that she later finds valuable in her husband’s country, and which she in turn passes on to the people, to the benefit of all.

The Old Woman of Dreams card reminds us that we should always take time to apprentice ourselves to the knowledge of our dreams. Although many of our dreams don’t make sense to us in a narrative context, nevertheless the characters who populate them and the images which appear hold information that might be helpful to us along our path. Our dreams also reflect the wisdom of our inner self: the part of us that knows what’s good for us even when our conscious mind does not.

cards.name: Cliff
cards.up:
Standing on the Edge
For most of us, there are many times during our lives when we feel that we're on a cliff edge. When we're caught in the midst of a crisis or standing on the brink of a major change. Will we try to hold tight, to keep all the pieces of our disintegrating life together? Or will we close our eyes, trust in the story that's unfolding, and let ourselves fall?
We can see the cliff edge as a place of terror or a place of opportunity. This card invites us to consider the ways in which we might transform our fear into a sense of evolving possibility. Sometimes, we're drawn to do certain things, to take certain steps, in spite of our fear of the consequences. But sometimes, the situation we're facing requires even more of us: we're asked to actively embrace our fear, and to take certain steps precisely because we're afraid.
The Cliff card, then, urges us to confront any fearful situation that we might be facing with our eyes wide open. What would happen if we recognized our fear and explored all the ways in which that fear was holding us back from the possibility of a more fulfilling life? What would happen if we took the step over the cliff edge because it scares us? Facing our fear is an opportunity for growth, and if we can face it with a sense of purpose, we'll feel that we're more in control of our own falling. And as a consequence, we'll become stronger, and more ready to face the inevitable challenges we'll meet along the path.

cards.name: Macha
cards.up:
Strength and Endurance
Macha was a ‘fairy wife,’ and probably the reflection of an old horse goddess, who came to a farmer in Ulster, Ireland, and married him, bringing fertility to his fields and health to his crops and herds.
Although she’d forbidden him to tell anyone about her, the farmer nevertheless boasted to the king of Ulster that his wife could run faster than any of the royal horses. As a consequence, the king forced Macha to race against his horses – even though she was pregnant with twins. She won, but she died at the finish line after giving birth to two healthy boys. Before she died, she laid a curse upon the men of Ulster that they would be overcome by the weakness and pain of a woman in childbirth when their enemies approached them in battle; it would remain so for nine generations.

Macha prompts us to remember the strength of women, and our capacity for endurance in the face of pain and hardship. But what we need on this Heroine’s Journey of ours isn’t just physical strength; we need the inner strength that comes from knowing that our life is important and valuable, and that we possess the determination to carry on along our Journey even when times get tough. Inner strength allows us to face difficult decisions without flinching, to take responsibility for ourselves and our own actions, and to understand that we’re the authors and narrators of our own story.

cards.name: Temptation
cards.up:
At some time during our Heroine's Journey, we'll come up against one or more great temptations; they're perhaps the greatest tests we'll have to endure. We might encounter situations or people who will seduce us away from our true path and lead us to make decisions which prevent us from completing the Journey.
Temptation often comes in the form of an easy way out, and in the form of things which, once upon a time, we wanted more than anything else. The seductive snare of an easy life: a nice house, a well-paid job; security rather than uncertainty. Sometimes it presents itself in the form of a possible partner who, while seeming very attractive, will hurt us, or who does not share the values we've come to espouse. Each one of these temptations will present itself to us with its own unique basket of quandaries, and it will be hard to navigate through the choices we'll need to make.
Sometimes we don't realize that we're being tempted; sometimes it seems as if we have no choices about the way forward. But we always have choices. This card reminds you to stop, and to consider those choices and their consequences when temptation arrives along the way.

cards.name: Sheela-Na-Gig
cards.up:
Fertility and Creativity
In Britain and Ireland, scattered among medieval churches, castles, holy wells, bridges, and town walls, you’ll find a surprisingly large number of stone carvings of women exposing their genitals, either pointing at their vulvas or holding them open with their hands. These figures are called Sheela-na-gigs. The upper half of their bodies are old and deathlike, with withered breasts, skeletal ribs, skull-like heads, and hollow eyes. But the lower half reminds us of a woman’s sexuality, her fertility, the act of giving birth.
These figures are believed to represent folk goddesses associated with fertility and childbirth – but also with the lands of the dead. In the oldest European traditions, the two attributes almost always go together. There are two sides of the ubiquitous Great Mother archetype: death and birth. Every life bears within it the seed of its own death – but no end is ever less than a new beginning.
As an ally along our Journey, the Sheela-na-gig is a midwife who reminds us of the energy and power of our creativity as women, and of the nature of our fertility, which changes over the course of our lives. Fertility isn’t just about giving birth to children, but about birthing all kinds of life into the world.

cards.name: The Wasteland
cards.up:
The Wasteland is the place where dreams go to die. It's an arid, rootless place, and its ground is infertile. In it, we're cut off from the source of life. We inhabit the Wasteland when we occupy ourselves with jobs that bring safety and security, but don't bring us meaning or joy.
The Wasteland is the place where we've allowed ourselves to become what we were never meant to be. Where, instead of following our own instincts, we'll spend most of our lives trying to make other people happy, squeezing ourselves into glass slippers that were made for them, not us, and living from our heads rather than our hearts. The Wasteland kills all that's alive and vibrant inside us.
Living in the Wasteland means that we're out of touch with the seasons and the cycles of the year, and with the natural world to which we've forgotten we belong. And when we lose our relationship with the land and the other-than-humans who inhabit it alongside us, then in the deepest sense, we lose ourselves too. Our exhaustion is bone-deep, and we come to believe that we're alone. This card invites you to discern all the ways in which you might still have one foot in the Wasteland today. How can you escape it? What needs to change in your life?

cards.name: The Threshold
cards.up:
The Threshold card ushers in the beginning of something, representing a frontier between what's gone before and whatever waits for us in the future. When we stand on the threshold, we apprentice ourselves to possibility.
The moment when you step onto the threshold isn't always a comfortable one. You'll be leaving behind the ground you know, and you're about to take a significant step into the unknown: nothing on the other side is familiar to you yet. It's the point of maximum pressure. Do you have the courage and resilience to step into unknown territory?
The Threshold card is reminiscent of the traditional monastic practice of statio, a term which is often used for the intermediate stages during a pilgrimage. Statio is an intentional pause. The individual is about to enter a sacred place but pauses first at the door to shed any burdens, worries, or other distractions which might get in the way of being truly present to the Divine.
This card, then, invites you to pause on the threshold, to take a deep breath, to contemplate this moment between moments – and then make the leap of faith which will bring you safely to the other side.

cards.name: Bean Feasa
cards.up:
Women’s Wisdom
The Wise Woman – the Bean Feasa (pronounced ‘Ban Fassa’), literally the ‘woman of knowledge’ – is a key figure in Celtic folklore. She’s a powerful healer whose methods extend beyond the practices of herbalism which are typically associated with the wise women of other traditions. The Bean Feasa would act as an intermediary between people and the Otherworld, so incorporating into her practice elements of both spiritual guide and modern therapeutic psychologist.
The Bean Feasa’s close association with the Otherworld can be seen as shamanic in nature, involving visits to the spirit world in order to return with gifts and knowledge. In this way, she was able to establish not just communication, but a kind of equilibrium between the two worlds which would in turn foster moral and spiritual equilibrium within her community.
As an ally on our Journey, the Bean Feasa offers us the old ancestral and spiritual wisdom which teaches us how we might live in balance in the world, and how we might live in harmony in our communities. She reminds us to listen to the whisperings of the Otherworld and shows us how to discern the true meaning and nature of events and situations, with all their multiple interconnections. With her help, we can discover the wisest courses of action, and the wisest decisions to take, along our path.

cards.name: Transformation
cards.up:
Transformation takes place as a consequence of difficult, testing initiatory experiences which are alchemical in nature. The ancient art of alchemy is centered on the ways in which one thing can be changed into another, and its goal is to perfect, purify, or profoundly evolve the material in question. In the Western mystery traditions, the achievement of gnosis – personal knowledge and enlightenment – was an important consequence of this process, which would eventually lead the individual to a sense of completeness and possibility.
Ultimately, transformation is the endpoint of the Heroine's Journey because transformation is the stuff of life. To be human means always to be growing, to be transforming – and we're all alchemists, deep inside.

It's only by allowing ourselves to be transformed that we can hope in turn to transform the world. If we want to change the dominant, life-denying cultural mythology which is failing us and failing the planet, we can begin by transforming the stories that each one of us chooses to live by. In the process, we'll uncover our personal calling, and discover the unique gift that we each bring to the world at this time. This card invites us to surrender ourselves to that profound process of never-ending becoming.

cards.name: Mis
cards.up:
Divine Madness
The old Irish story of Mis (pronounced ‘Mish’) tells of a woman who, driven mad by grief and the horrors of war, grows fur and feathers. She flies away into the hills and woods, eats wild and raw food, and leaves the intolerable world behind her. Mis, then, represents the woman who cannot and will not submit to the brutalities of the world around her. She withdraws from ‘civilization’ and takes solace in the natural world.
In the extremity of some great grief or trauma, the archetypal madwoman or Wild Woman inside us might break out. And at such times in our lives, it might be a good thing to allow ourselves to break and run for the simple solitude of the hills, to withdraw from the unendurable everyday. To safely express our rage and lick our bleeding wounds, and to allow the natural world to work its healing magic on us. Because this disintegration of our civilized, socialized selves forces us to uncover, in the depths of our extremity, whatever it is that we believe to be the source of life.
Mis is the original Wild Woman, speaking for us all: for the rage which we cannot express, for the grief which eats our heart out, for the voices we’ve suppressed out of fear. Ultimately, Mis is healed by love and gentleness and, as a consequence, is able to return to the world with new strength and focus.

cards.name: The Descent
cards.up:
The Descent, in which we seek out and ultimately stand before the judgment of the dark goddess in the Underworld, destroys outdated forms of living and being. It prepares the ground for the wisdom we need to give birth to our most authentic self – the self that knows its place in the world and fully belongs. This descent cannot be avoided, because the Heroine's Journey requires us to make a sacrifice before we might continue on our path. We're asked to sacrifice our old upper-world self: all the parts of us which once were preserved by our attachment to what we now understand to be the Wasteland.
There, in the relentless dark, the ego begins to be dismantled. We'll be taken apart, broken into pieces, so that we can begin the long, hard work of putting the fragments back together again, and rebirthing ourselves into a new and more authentic pattern.

There's no escaping this process, and it can be hard. But in that place of destruction, gestation, and rebirth, we'll begin to explore the biggest question of all: if we strip away everything we're told we must be, what's left? When we choose to let go of everything that once we imagined defined us and mattered to us, what then might we become?

cards.name: Forest
cards.up:
Finding the Path
The forests of northern European fairy tales are dark, dangerous places, abundant with disconcerting shadows and populated by tightly packed trees. They represent a world beyond the village, the community: an Otherworld, steeped in myth and magic, which lies outside of normal human experience. Usually, the darkwood is the home of witches and monsters, personifying all the fears of the collective unconscious.
When you enter the forest, you're accepting the inevitability of transformation. Something is going to change. Something may be lost, but something – if you embark on the journey with a true heart and a willingness to learn – will always be gained. This card invites you to trust in the bone-deep alchemy of metamorphosis, and to take the plunge into the unknown.
Once you find yourself caught up in the formidable entanglements of the forest, it's not always clear – especially when choices have to be made – which path you should take. Often, it's the overgrown path – the one which looks to be the darkest, the least promising – which will lead you to what you're looking for. And sometimes there's no obvious path at all and you're forced to forge your own way through the trees.
Even in the loneliest of forests, though, there are allies and helpers to be found – if you're paying attention. But be sure to look closely, and don't jump to the obvious conclusions. A wolf isn't always going to eat you, and the old woman carrying her basket of berries isn't always a witch. Treasure the tiniest traces of light, because even in the darkest forests, there's hope to be found.

cards.name: Moor
cards.up:
Silence and Simplicity
Moorland is characterized by its lack of trees and its low-growing, uncultivated vegetation. Usually, moors occupy high ground. They offer us an evocative expanse, a sweeping vista, a sense of remoteness; the combination of elevation and openness means that they're often very windy places.
The uncluttered simplicity of the moor makes it a landscape to which we might come to achieve clarity. We can breathe deeply and more easily here, in the clear air and the land which sweeps all the way to the far, wide horizon. The cleansing wind clears away mental clutter, breaks down the rigidity of customary thought patterns, frees us from the structures of civilization which both define and confine us. Space is created for new insights and understandings. Our imagination is unshackled, released into a timeless, flexible, and magical sphere.
The solitude of the moor can sometimes make us feel uncomfortable, but this card invites us to embrace the silence. Here, we can learn the art of deep listening and deep sensing. What does the wind have to whisper to you? What patterns can you see in the looming storm clouds? When the jumbled detritus of everyday life is blown away, what remains? And how does that make you feel?

cards.name: Immram
cards.up:
IMMRAM
Immram, in Irish, literally means 'rowing about.' In the old tales which were referred to as immrama, the protagonist (always a man, and usually a cleric or a penitent) would set off across the sea in a simple coracle (a small, round boat made of animal hide) with no particular direction in mind. The purpose of the expedition was simply to see where God would lead them. If we undertake an immram, then, we give ourselves over to fate. There's no preordained destination – and so an immram is, above all, about trusting whatever life might have in store for us.
There's no map for this particular Journey; there's no fixed path. And at certain times in our lives that might be a good and a necessary thing because following the paths that others have set for us, the paths that the over-culture confines us to, can be the cause of many problems.
Those earlier paths might not reflect who we really feel we are, but although we often know that something in our life needs to change, we don't always know what that change should look like. This is a journey, then, in which we simply leave. We step out of the door, put one foot in front of the other, grit our teeth, and walk. We trust in fate, or the gods, to point us in the right direction.

cards.name: Quest
cards.up:
The quest is a directed journey with a distinct purpose or goal – a pot of gold, a home, the answer to a mystery – which is clear from the beginning, even if the precise trajectory of the journey doesn't always work out exactly the way it might have been planned.
The Hero's Journey, as identified by the American mythologist Joseph Campbell, is primarily a quest narrative, as are sagas such as the Epic of Gilgamesh and the Odyssey. Perhaps the most common kind of narrative in myth and folklore around the world, it typically requires the Heroine to overcome a series of obstacles, or pass a series of tests, to achieve her heart's desire or to undergo a necessary transformation.
Sometimes, the Heroine who sets out on a quest has no more definite aim than to 'seek her fortune,'

and sometimes she might be cast out of her home rather than embarking on her Journey voluntarily. But at some point, soon after her departure, she'll learn of something that will transform her initial wanderings into a quest.
If the shape of your Journey looks as if it might be a quest, always be sure that you really want whatever it is that you're looking for; and also be careful that you haven't been sent on a 'false quest' by someone else. Be honest with yourself: is your stated reason for setting out on your Journey the real reason?

cards.name: Old Crane Woman
cards.up:
Guardian of the Threshold
In Celtic mythology, cranes are associated with old women. They guard the treasures of the Otherworld and the entrances to Otherworldly abodes. Like the heron, the crane's ability to move between water, land, and air makes her a symbol of shape-shifting and magic; she's a powerful and a liminal bird who acts as a guide to those who wish to travel through the borderlands.
In the course of any journey, we'll arrive at one or more thresholds which separate one place – one world – from another. They are transition points into new ways of being. And all such thresholds have their guardians, who ensure that those who approach are equipped for the crossing. The Guardian of the Threshold isn't necessarily a menacing monster who might bite off your head – but she's not to be messed with, either. Her
judgement is final: you're either ready for this new adventure or you're not.
Old Crane Woman is something of a contradiction: she has the wildness of a bird, but the steadiness of a wise old woman. Her decision about your suitability for the challenges ahead will depend upon how you approach her, and chances are she'll have a test for you: a question, or a riddle to solve. But the Guardian of the Threshold isn't your adversary; if you're ready for the crossing, she's the one who will show you the way. Old Crane Woman – if you ask her nicely and are sure to pay your respects – is your soul guide. In this card, she invites you to step forward to answer her questions about your readiness for the Journey ahead, and to reveal to her the essence of who you are.

cards.name: The Sacred Marriage
cards.up:
The Heroine's Journey requires us above all to reclaim the creative and generative feminine energy buried inside each of us. But before we can fully orient ourselves to the final stage of our Journey – our return to the world with the gifts we amassed along the way – we also need to work on integrating and harmonizing the masculine qualities which each of us possesses.
This is the Sacred Marriage, in Celtic traditions, between the goddess Sovereignty and the king; it's the hieros gamos, the sacred marriage of masculine and feminine which is also the goal of alchemy. It's necessary because, in seeking to restore the feminine to our culture, we must not lose sight of the fact that the cause of our problems isn't the presence of masculine qualities in the world, but rather that those qualities have become excessively dominant.

The qualities that we might think of as feminine include an awareness of the gifts of embodiment, as well as intuitive, emotional, and empathic ways of being in the world. In contrast, the qualities we think of as masculine are active, rational, goal-oriented, and structuring, and are traditionally associated with the intellect and the spirit. Harmonizing these different energies within ourselves is a prerequisite for the work of restoring balance to an outer world which has lost its equilibrium, and this card invites each of us to find our own unique ways of working with and balancing these qualities.

cards.name: Stone Cirlce
cards.up:
The Sacred Landscape
Our ancestors constructed a surprisingly large number of stone circles throughout Europe. Research suggests that they functioned both as astronomical observatories and as centers for ceremony. These two functions are related to each other: stone circles represent the ancient belief that celestial objects and their cycles of movement might exert subtle influences on human behavior, as well as on the health and well-being of the land below. Our ancestors believed in an interconnected cosmos in which we were one part of a complex, living whole. This card, then, reminds us of that interconnectivity.
The ceremonies which took place at such sacred sites are likely to have been associated with specific times in the cycle of the solar year; many stone circles are aligned with the position of the Sun at equinoxes or solstices. Our ancestors lived in a way which celebrated the cycles and seasons of the land, of the natural world of which they were a part, and of the living cosmos around them.
This card emphasizes the need to recognize and honor the cycles and seasons of our own bodies and our own lives. The body is also a sacred site; in what ways might you bring yourself into greater attunement with yours? How might you recognize its need for rest at certain times, and delight in its strength and energy at others? The body, in a very real sense, is our soulmate. Our Journey through life depends on it: the body is literally the ground of our being. This card invites us to consider that ground as sacred.

cards.name: Bridge
cards.up:
The Place between Worlds
The bridge in this card is an in-between place. On one side of the chasm lies the mundane world and the life we know we've now outgrown. On the other side, the Otherworld shimmers, alight with promise and possibility. The bridge invites us to step over. But do we really believe in that magical new world across the water? Do we really believe it will be quite so bright and shiny after we've crossed?
The bridge is a point of transition from one place to another, or from one way of being to another. It's a liminal place – a place between stories – where the old story is fading, and a new one is waiting to emerge. Its invitations are manifold, as we hover on the brink of profound transformation – but as we stand there on the bridge, we're asked to embrace uncertainty. This is a time of waiting, of not quite knowing the future. Can we trust in a possible future, anyway? Is that magical land really as good as it looks? Can we accept the risk of leaving our known, safe, and familiar old world behind, and make the decision to cross to the indeterminate new one?
The Bridge card calls on us to believe – in the possibility of a new world and a new life, and in the new story that's unfolding before our eyes. In one sense, what's required is a leap of faith. The structure of the bridge is solid and sure beneath our feet, but we can only know this once we've taken the first step to cross it.

cards.name: Labyrinth
cards.up:
LABYRINTH
During the Middle Ages, the practice of walking the labyrinth at great Christian sites like Chartres in France became entangled with the pilgrimage tradition. Labyrinths created in the stone floors of cathedrals were often the final landmark on a pilgrim's path and so became a symbol for the spiritual journey which they had undertaken, assisting with the process of integration.
The Labyrinth card reminds us that life is not a linear journey. But its single path leads ultimately to the center: the path with heart. The good news is that labyrinths aren't mazes: they're designed to help you find your way to the center. They're designed precisely to center us. Because walking the labyrinth lifts us out of the everyday world for a while, and fosters contemplation. And there, at the center of the labyrinth, you'll discover new insights, uncover old wisdom, or gain new knowledge. You'll begin to understand why it was that you decided to walk this path. Then it will be time to make your way out of the labyrinth, taking into the world the gifts that you received in the center.

cards.name: Bog
cards.up:
Stagnation
Boglands are profoundly still and silent places; in them, time hardly seems to pass at all. Decay and decomposition are also suspended there, so our ancestors buried bodies deep in the moist peat to preserve them. If you reach your hands down into that rich, black butter, who knows what buried mysteries you might find. To love a bog, then, is to love secrecy and subtlety, to forage for what lies hidden beneath the surface.
Superficially, a bog might seem like a dark and bleak place. And yet, if you choose to look closely, it will reveal an abundance of subtle color, of texture, and of life. It won't shout out at you, like a flower garden or a rainforest; a bog will creep up on you and offer up its gifts one or two at a time. In this way, you come to see them more clearly and know them more deeply, because there's little else to crowd them out. A bog, then, teaches us to look for treasure in the most unlikely places: to focus on the close-up, the quiet, the seemingly obscure.
But above all, this card asks us to understand that sometimes, what appears to be stagnation is actually preservation. There are times when we need to hold still, to preserve our energy and life force. There are times when we need to rest our assaulted senses, to cut back and pare down, to reduce our tendency for overwhelm, and to drink in the beauty of the everyday.

cards.name: Peregrina
cards.up:
This card represents the Peregrina – the pilgrim, the Heroine at the beginning of her Journey. She’s looking for something, though she doesn’t yet know what it is. Like the Fool in the tarot, she represents innocence: she’s open, curious, and ready to embrace life. And yet, she’s cloaked and clothed for heavy weather: for a journey which may turn out to be arduous, in the end.

As she walks through this wild terrain, far from the civilization of which she was once a part, the Peregrina is shedding the ties which usually bind her; she’s discovering a willingness to live in the present and to have no presumptions about the nature of what might follow.

Happily, she isn’t undergoing this journey alone; her companions travel with her. Because, in the old traditions of Classical Europe, the idea existed that each of us comes into this world accompanied by a soul guide: a daimon, in the Greek tradition. The soul guide is always trying to help us to remember who we are and why we chose to come here; it reminds us of our calling, the great gift that we came to offer the world in troubling times.

This card reminds us that this is the ultimate goal of our journey: we must be willing to detach from who we’ve been, and what we might become, before we can discover who we’re really meant to be and what our work is in the world.

cards.name: Stinging Nettle
cards.up:
10. STINGING NETTLE
​Rethink restriction
​Botanical name: Urtica dioica.
​Energy: verdant and nurturing.
​Other names: common nettle, lesser nettle.
​Traditional/medicinal uses: the juice makes a fortifying tonic that helps with gout, anemia and kidney problems.
​Magickal/historical uses: they are used in spells for protection and fertility. Nettles are nutritionally dense plants that can be used to make delicious soups, beers and wines.
​THE POISON
Stinging Nettle has decided to cut a few things from their diet in a bid to become healthier. It all starts innocently enough: for the first few weeks their willpower is strong, and it’s going so well they decide to restrict a few more items. Then the restriction becomes a game to see how long they can stretch the time between meals. Stinging Nettle’s world becomes a narrow focus of restraint and never quite feeling full enough, but they think about food all the time. Meals out with family and friends become joyless tasks filled with anxiety, because restriction has led to obsession.
​THE ANTIDOTE
The human body is such a clever machine, knowing intuitively when and what to eat and when to stop. Taste buds become dulled once the stomach registers fullness. Restrictive diets don’t give long-term results, and constraint and control around food steals joy and comes at too high a price. Stinging Nettle can rethink restriction and relax into the idea that their body knows best, and if they let it guide them then hunger and fullness become second nature. Weight doesn’t necessarily correlate to health. One of the delightful things about having a corporeal body is the full enjoyment of food and drink while on earth.

cards.name: Destroying Angel
cards.up:
1. DESTROYING ANGEL
​Soul contracts
​Botanical name: Amanita virosa.
​Energy: detached and merciless.
​Other names: European destroying angel amanita.
​Traditional/medicinal uses: as with Deathcap (card 2), Destroying Angel’s medicinal potential is being researched.
​Magickal/historical uses: no known magickal uses. No known antidote if ingested; it shows no mercy.
​THE POISON
Destroying Angel has been wronged and is filled with a righteous wrath. They will stop at nothing to make sure that the person who has crossed them will suffer. Like an avenging angel, they are consumed with fury and will give no quarter; however, the punishment they seek outweighs the crime. They are not thinking rationally, and deliberately go out of their way to hurt someone. Onlookers can understand why they feel this way but are starting to wonder if Destroying Angel has taken it too far.
​THE ANTIDOTE
There’s a reason why Destroying Angel’s enemy has stirred up so much emotion: they are soul bound and were contracted to meet and challenge each other before they incarnated on earth. By putting so much energy into retribution, Destroying Angel’s bond to their nemesis becomes stronger and more constrictive. For them to end the connection they can visualise ripping up the soul contract and saying: ‘I release you. We are no longer bound. Our contract is null and void.’ They will find that the ire will dissipate and they will start to dissociate from their enemy. While the actions of their enemy are never condoned, the hold over Destroying Angel will be lessened and they will, at last, find peace.

cards.name: Yew
cards.up:
35. YEW
​Embrace change
​Botanical name: 
Taxus baccata
​Energy: 
hallowed and resurrecting
​Other names: 
common yew, English yew
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: 
It is used in some homeopathic remedies.
​Magickal / Historical uses: 
It is a sacred Druidical tree and a symbol of life after death. A storm once upended an ancient yew tree in an English churchyard, and the next day entwined within its exposed roots were the bones of the long dead.
​The Poison: 
Yew is stuck in grief and cannot imagine ever being joyful again. Long ago they lost something or someone dear to them and it colours every aspect of their life. They are mired in their sorrow, which has become like a pair of comfortable old shoes. They feel they can never be happy again and cannot accept the changes the loss has brought them. In their darkest moments they feel that no one else has suffered as much as them, that they have suffered the most.
​The Antidote: 
One thing people can always rely on is change, because life is in constant flux and can transform in an instant. From a limited perspective our human part detests change and will do anything to maintain the status quo, but resistance is futile: life will change as we grow. Yew will enjoy gains and suffer losses, and the more they can accept this as part of life on earth the more they will enjoy the crazy ride. They can set down the heavy load of being a hapless victim beholden to fate by embracing change, realising that everything is just as it should be. As Apollinaire said: 'After each sorrow, joy came back again.'

cards.name: Black Bryony
cards.up:
28. BLACK BRYONY
​Catharsis
​Botanical name: Tamus communis or Dioscorea communis
​Energy: irritating and purging
​Other names: blackeye root, black bindweed, lady's seal
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Fresh root was applied topically as a poultice to clear up bruises and inflammation.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Used to banish negative energy, purge stale influences, and bring in the new.
​The Poison: 
Feeling powerless or unable to express anger safely, masking it behind a friendly appearance while rage simmers underneath. The suppressed anger eventually creeps up as outbursts, overreactions, or physical ailments.
​The Antidote: 
Recognizing anger as a pure gift pointing to unresolved issues or violated boundaries. Meditating to uncover past hurts, expressing anger safely, and experiencing a cathartic healing process.

cards.name: Cherry Laurel
cards.up:
34. CHERRY LAUREL
​Peacekeeper
​Botanical name: Prunus laurocerasus
​Energy: bitter and crystalline
​Other names: English laurel, common laurel
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: It was used as a sedative to bring relief from insomnia and night coughs. The poisonous parts of the plants are the leaves, which contain small amounts of the deadly hydrocyanic acid.
​Magickal / Historical uses: The tree is used in protection and love spells.
​The Poison:
 The disempowered Cherry Laurel tries to keep the peace at all costs. If someone is upset they believe it is their personal responsibility to calm things down and make them right. They avoid confrontation and are always the first one to yield, which leads to them being taken advantage of. Their feelings do not appear to matter, getting brushed aside and eclipsed by louder and more aggressive personalities. Cherry Laurel feels as though they are walking on eggshells with someone, which affects their health.
​The Antidote:
Cherry Laurel has a natural calming energy, which makes them an ideal peacekeeper: a useful skill. However, they constantly misuse this ability by capitulating to a loved one. They can feel bitterness creeping in because their needs are always being ignored. Cherry Laurel is allowed to speak up and tell others if they feel they are being mistreated, even if this disturbs the peace and causes conflict. In fact, it is sometimes necessary. They say 'Choose your battles', and in this case Cherry Laurel must fight.

cards.name: Mistletoe
cards.up:
16. MISTLETOE
​Interdependence
​Botanical name: Viscum album
​Energy: strengthening and fortifying
​Other names: herbe de la Croix, lignum crucis, mystyldene
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: In 17th-century herbalism, a tonic of the leaves and twigs was suggested to calm nerves and muscles.
​Magickal / Historical uses: A sacred plant to the Druids, used to banish negativity and invite blessings for the new year. As a parasitic plant, it forms a symbiotic link with its host tree.
​The Poison:
Represents extreme hyper-independence, refusing help from others out of a belief that asking for assistance is a sign of weakness.
​The Antidote:
Teaches that human beings are naturally interconnected and interdependent. Accepting help and trusting others is a key part of living a balanced life.

cards.name: Baneberry
cards.up:
6. BANEBERRY
​Just ask!
​Botanical name: Actaea spicata.
​Energy: lurking, concealed and expelling.
​Other names: bugbane, herb Christopher, toadroot.
​Traditional/medicinal uses: the root has been used in folk remedies to treat headaches, coughs, colds and joint inflammation. The berries are extremely poisonous when ingested but can be used to make a rich, black dye when crushed and macerated.
​Magickal/historical uses: it can be used in binding spells. The plant has a peculiar, odious smell that is very attractive to toads.
​THE POISON
Baneberry has seen bossy and demanding people get their own way and does not like this behaviour, so they will act meek and compliant to feel superior. They will nod and smile and say everything is okay when asked but later complain about not being considered. They will also sneakily go behind people’s backs to get their way. Baneberry is quite manipulative and doesn’t like asking for what they want outright. They conceal their needs and desires by hinting and indirect questioning, but all they really need to do is just ask!
​THE ANTIDOTE
It’s true that being bossy and demanding isn’t nice, but neither is it good to be meek and sneaky. This plant medicine is a lesson in speaking up and not hiding your wants and needs. Baneberry is allowed to state what they want and would like. We all are but then we let it go, knowing that we have stated our case and that our preferences have been heard and may be considered. Baneberry has expressed and been true to themselves, and in the end this is what really matters.

cards.name: Hemlock
cards.up:
32. HEMLOCK
​Psychic protection
​Botanical name: Conium maculatum
​Energy: hypnotic and pacifying
​Other names: herb bennet, poison hemlock, poison parsley, spotted hemlock, warlock's weed
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Although extremely poisonous, in ancient times it was carefully prepared as a sedative for the nerves.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Long associated with witches and witchcraft, it is a herb sacred to the goddess of witches Hekate. It is used in spells for protection and purifying
​The Poison:
Hemlock feels emotionally drained and physically exhausted after work and social interactions, often suffering from migraines. They leave themselves open to physical and spiritual energy vampires, as these individuals are attracted to their bright and open energy. The disempowered Hemlock lives in fear. They have dabbled with contacting the spirit world, but unfortunately did not prepare themselves properly and left their thoughts open to lower entities that thrive upon an anxious and worried mind.
​The Antidote: 
Before beginning any psychic work Hemlock can call upon Archangel Michael for protection. By imagining being bathed in a beam of electric blue light from this powerful angel they can burn away the detritus of human worries and feel the calmness of their soul taking charge. As an antidote to their exhausting social interactions they can imagine a beautiful bright bubble of white light around them and call in their guides and angels as a light shield throughout the day.

cards.name: Fry Agaric
cards.up:
18. FLY AGARIC
​Virtual reality
​Botanical name: Amanita muscaria
​Energy: enchanting, playful, and psychedelic
​Other names: fly amanita
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Used in Eastern Europe and parts of Russia as an anti-inflammatory and pain reliever. Preliminary research explores its potential regarding cognitive decline.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Associated with fairies and magic. Historically used by Siberian shamans to induce visions to guide their communities.
​The Poison: 
Refusing to engage with everyday societal expectations or daily life, treating the real world with detachment or cynicism while ignoring practical responsibilities.
​The Antidote:
Encourages observing life's "game" with a sense of wonder, humor, and detachment, viewing earth as an experience for the soul's growth while remaining lighthearted.

cards.name: Madonna Lily
cards.up:
25. MADONNA LILY
​Spiritual superiority
​Botanical name: Lilium candidum
​Energy: perfect, pure, and mystical
​Other names: lily of the field, white lily
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Bulbs were used in folk remedies to create a poultice for burns, ulcers, bruises, and skin conditions.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Dedicated to Mother Mary, symbolizing purity and innocence.
​The Poison:
A disempowered state of feeling spiritually superior, judgment, and righteous indignation. Believing oneself to be cleaner, purer, or more evolved than others, while acting as a disapproving figure.
​The Antidote: 
Remembering that judging others is an ego trap. Realizing every soul is on its own evolutionary journey doing its best, and helping others feel good without judgment.

cards.name: Henbane
cards.up:
27. HENBANE
​Away with the fae
​Botanical name: Hyoscyamus niger
​Energy: soporific and hypnotic
​Other names: black henbane, hog's bean, stinking nightshade
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Used in modern medicine to treat epilepsy and Parkinson's disease, and in folk remedies for headaches.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Dried leaves were added to festival beers for an extra narcotic kick to escape the rigors of reality.
​The Poison:
Living with feet firmly planted in mid-air, detached from normal rules of reality. Preferring escapism, daydreaming, and living "away with the fairies" over being present in everyday life.
​The Antidote: 
Grounding oneself into human form and the present moment. Visualizing a connection to the earth's core (via the solar plexus) to remain fully present, awake, and joyfully connected with others.

cards.name: Larkspur
cards.up:
24. LARKSPUR
​Bright star
​Botanical name: Consolida regalis
​Energy: wild, inky, and cathartic
​Other names: field larkspur, lark's claw, knight's spur
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Anecdotally, the juice of the leaves and flowers can help heal wounds.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Grows wild in the fields of Europe and can be employed in protection spells. Its bluish-purple, star-shaped flowers signify joy and a pure heart.
​The Poison:
Never really fitting in, feeling branded as weird or an outcast, and becoming a loner. Unable to comprehend human violence and unkindness, becoming insular and loathing to engage with the world.
​The Antidote:
Remembering the purpose to help and heal humanity rather than hide from it. Bringing creativity, joy, and bright energy into any room unapologetically like a bright star in the sky.

cards.name: Belladonna
cards.up:
22. BELLADONNA
​Accept your fate
​Botanical name: Atropa belladonna
​Energy: fated, sedated, and glamorous
​Other names: deadly nightshade, devil's cherries
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Used in the treatment of eye diseases and as a powerful muscle relaxant. Its sedating effect makes people seem unaffected by strong emotion.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Associated with Atropos, one of the three Greek Fates who preside over human life. 'Bella donna' is Italian for 'beautiful woman'; its energy is perfect for glamour and beauty spells.
​The Poison:
Has a bad habit of running away from accountability and escaping into a dream. Coping with difficult feelings by putting off simple tasks and flaking out on responsibilities.
​The Antidote: 
Working through uncomfortable emotions directly by feeling them completely rather than dodging them. Accepting fate, facing responsibilities, and allowing oneself and others to express messy feelings cleanly.

cards.name: Mandrake
cards.up:
26. MANDRAKE
​Obsession
​Botanical name: Mandragora officinarum
​Energy: intense and possessive
​Other names: Satan's apple, mandragora
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: The root was used to create a sleeping draught for physical pain.
​Magickal / Historical uses: An ingredient in flying ointments, hallucinogenic brews, love spells, aphrodisiacs, and rituals to drive away evil spirits.
​The Poison: 
Chasing the continuous dopamine hit of new relationships or quick thrill fixes. Getting bored easily when stability settles in, discarding lovers or friends, and entering destructive obsession cycles.
​The Antidote: 
Spending time alone to bypass the constant distraction of intense relationships. Engaging in the inner work of self-knowledge so meaningless obsessions fall away and inner peace takes over.

cards.name: Snowdrop
cards.up:
9. SNOWDROP
​Go with the flow
​Botanical name: Galanthus nivalis.
​Energy: opening and stimulating.
​Other names: fair maid of February.
​Traditional/medicinal uses: it contains a substance called galanthamine, which has been proven useful in managing certain forms of dementia.
​Magickal/historical uses: the first flower to appear after winter, they herald the return of light and warmth and are a symbol of rebirth and the triumph of light over dark.
​THE POISON
Snowdrop has a hard time accepting the cycles of life. When things are going well they worry that something bad will happen. When things are going badly they think the good times will never arrive again. Snowdrop is stuck in a pessimistic thought frequency and always expects the worst to happen. They focus on the negative and forget to be grateful for what they already have.
​THE ANTIDOTE
It’s the nature of life to have its ups and downs, and the best way for Snowdrop to deal with this is to pretend that life is a river and they are a leaf just going with the flow. Sometimes the way will be rocky and difficult and other times it will be plain sailing. Release the need to control outside influences and go with the flow of life’s journey. Snowdrop can listen to the whispers of their guardian angel. It’s all part of the polarities of life on earth – the opposites, the good and the bad: one cannot be appreciated without the other. Enjoy the good times, and when the bad times come know they will not last and the light will come back into life.

cards.name: Giant Hogweed
cards.up:
17. GIANT HOGWEED
​In/tolerance
​Botanical name: Heracleum mantegazzianum
​Energy: looming, scorching, and strange
​Other names: giant cow parsley, hogsbane
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Folk remedies used a decoction of seeds to treat skin conditions.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Used in healing and restorative spells as a plant that quickly exerts control over its environment.
​The Poison: 
Displays intolerance toward other people's views and a need to control situations or force one's own desires on those around them.
​The Antidote:
Reminds us that we can only control our own actions, thoughts, and boundaries. Urges practicing tolerance, stepping back, and allowing others to take charge.

cards.name: Narcissus
cards.up:
29. NARCISSUS
​Walk away
​Botanical name: Narcissus pseudonarcissus
​Energy: gilded and banishing
​Other names: wild daffodil, Lent lily
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Focuses on the compound galantamine, which helps slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Used in love and money spells for its sunny color; caution is taken as the flowers hide poisonous bulbs.
​The Poison:
Encountering emotional manipulation, lack of empathy, playing the victim, pushing buttons, and creating toxic cliques.
​The Antidote:
Recognizing the futility of chasing or trying to change a toxic person. Walking away, letting go of misplaced loyalty, and seeking relationships where mutual respect and peace exist.

cards.name: Cuckoo-pint
cards.up:
14. CUCKOO-PINT
​Sovereign boundaries
​Botanical name: Arum maculatum
​Energy: striking and restorative
​Other names: arum, lords and ladies, wake robin
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: The dried root was mixed with honey and taken as a stimulant for those weakened by illness.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Used to balance masculine and feminine energies and promote harmonious relationships.
​The Poison:
Describes a lack of personal boundaries, where someone constantly over-commits and says "yes" to help others—even when exhausted—leading to resentment and burnout.
​The Antidote:
Highlights the importance of setting boundaries, learning to say "no," and protecting one's personal time and energy before attempting to care for others.

cards.name: Holly
cards.up:
33. HOLLY
​Allow wealth
​Botanical name: Ilex aquifolium
​Energy: glossy, crimson and spiked
​Other names: common holly, holm, holy tree, Christ's thorn
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: The leaves have been used to treat fevers, jaundice and broken bones in the form of tinctures and poultices. Its poison reputation comes from the berries, which are violently purgative.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Associated with the winter solstice and the festival of Yule, it is an evergreen that symbolises new life. If brought into the home during winter it brings wealth and good luck.
​The Poison:
The disempowered Holly is jealous of the good fortune of others. They like to judge other people's spending habits on nice things or lavish holidays, often stating these people would be better off donating to charity. They become very envious and deeply feel the lack of indulgence in their own life, choosing to be offended by displays of wealth – which makes them very unhappy. There's nothing wrong with Holly wanting good fortune and comfort for themselves, but their poisonous behaviour demeans others for the enjoyment of wealth. They feel righteous when they disapprove of other people's prosperity, which makes them feel better about their own feelings of lack.
​The Antidote:
Holly can give themselves permission to enjoy little luxuries without breaking the bank. They can accept that having money does not make you a bad person but instead adds to the enjoyment of life and helps others. They must realise that other people's finances are none of their business and concentrate on their own wealth. Rejoicing in the good fortune of others and imagining prosperity for themselves opens channels for receiving. Holly deserves more and can practise allowing more.

cards.name: Hemlock Water-Dropwort
cards.up:
3. HEMLOCK WATER-DROPWORT
​Trust that feeling
​Botanical name: Oenanthe crocata.
​Energy: quick, virulent and starting.
​Other names: dead man's fingers, water-hemlock.
​Traditional/medicinal uses: it was used in poultices to clean wounds but it is not employed in modern medicine.
​Magickal/historical uses: no known magickal uses. A popular poison in ancient times, it affects the facial muscles and leaves its victims with a startling grin often called a 'sardonic smile'.
​THE POISON
A sardonic grin is a smile that never travels to the eyes; therefore, not everything is as it seems. Dropwort hides behind a seemingly innocuous facade, but once you scratch the surface things can get ugly. Dropwort wears a mask of niceness and faux concern that leaves you wondering why you feel uncomfortable in Dropwort’s presence despite the pleasant character. Could it be because they are saying lovely things, socially acceptable things, while all the time wishing you ill with their thoughts?
​THE ANTIDOTE
Discernment is so important when you interact with characters such as Dropwort. Do not rely on Dropwort’s words and how they present themselves. Instead, rely on how they make you feel. If you walk away feeling exhausted after Dropwort has been love bombing you then alarm bells should be ringing. Even if the logical conclusion says they have your best interests at heart or you still feel uneasy, learn to trust that feeling for it will always steer you right. Dropwort's games do not need to be played.

cards.name: Castor Bean
cards.up:
31. CASTOR BEAN
​Release the past
​Botanical name: Ricinus communis
​Energy: slippery and cathartic
​Other names: castor oil plant, palma christi
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Made from the seeds, castor oil is a well-known laxative because of its purgative nature. When applied topically it can help heal skin conditions.
​Magickal / Historical uses: The oil is used in spells to repel negative vibes and banish bad habits.
​The Poison:
Castor Bean obsesses about the past, focusing on how things used to be instead of concentrating on the here and now. Prone to wistfulness, they believe that things were better back then, remembering only the good times, and have a tendency to hoard physical items. They often put past lovers on a pedestal. This behaviour causes pain for their current and future partners, who believe that if only they exhibited the same qualities Castor Bean would love them more. Castor is beholden to the long ago.
​The Antidote: 
It is draining being in a relationship with an emotionally unavailable person whose head is stuck in bygone days. It's not anyone's sole responsibility to make someone happy, especially those infatuated with the ghosts of the past. Castor Bean obsessing about what could or might have been has become a life stealer and they need to release the past. The universe works in mysterious ways, and if Castor Bean was truly meant to be with someone they would be. There can be no other way.

cards.name: Lily Of The Valley
cards.up:
7. LILY OF THE VALLEY
​Open your heart
​Botanical name: Convallaria majalis.
​Energy: comforting, heady and perfumed.
​Other names: Jacob’s ladder, our lady’s tears.
​Traditional/medicinal uses: the plant was used in medicines to treat weak hearts; however, the active compound is now manufactured in a laboratory.
​Magickal/historical uses: it is often used in love spells. It’s known for its ephemeral nature, because once picked it will last just one day.
​THE POISON
Lily has closed their heart. They no longer want to get close to others, because they know they will just end up being hurt. Lily knows that nothing lasts and feels that the pain of losing someone is not worth the love they have invested. Lily has convinced themselves that being alone is best, so they push people away and will not pursue relationships even though this will bring them much joy.
​THE ANTIDOTE
Love is all there is. The nature of life on earth is ephemeral and nothing lasts forever, which is one of the hardest lessons to learn. We are here to make connections with others, and while they may not last in the physical world we will see each other again in the spirit world. Those we have loved and lost will be there, waiting for us when it is our turn to leave this earthly realm. Even those who have hurt us we will make amends with, and the joy of connection will be felt once again. Once Lily realises this they will find a beautiful world of emotional riches waiting for them.

cards.name: Opium Poppy
cards.up:
21. OPIUM POPPY
​Share your light
​Botanical name: Papaver somniferum
​Energy: sedating and escaping
​Other names: breadseed poppy
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: The narcotic sap has a hypnotic and sedative effect and is used to calm emotional and physical pain. Derivatives include morphine, codeine, and heroin.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Known to induce fantastical creative visions and spark innovative ideas. Spellworkers can work with the energy of the plant to manifest new ways of seeing things.
​The Poison: 
Dislikes interacting with others and avoids them as much as possible due to finding human behavior and social norms baffling. Prefers an insular lifestyle with little disturbance from outside influences.
​The Antidote: 
Encounters are meant to raise energy through interacting with others and sharing light. Encourages being more generous with time and energy while practicing grounding techniques (releasing outside energy and recalling one's own light on the out-breath) to stay balanced.

cards.name: Monkshood
cards.up:
23. MONKSHOOD
​Witchcraft
​Botanical name: Aconitum napellus
​Energy: poisonous, pernicious, and paralysing
​Other names: aconite, devil's bane, queen of poison, Venus's chariot, wolfsbane
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Folk remedies used it to create a soothing topical salve for muscle and nerve pain.
​Magickal / Historical uses: So called because its strange flowers resemble the hood of a medieval monk's cloak. Associated with Hekate, the goddess of witchcraft and magick.
​The Poison:
Highlights feelings of loneliness and censure; brings up feelings of not belonging, being victimized, misrepresented, and misunderstood. Carries memories of being persecuted or burned at the stake for possessing powerful secret knowledge.
​The Antidote: 
Retreating from the maddening crowd to rest, decompress, and recharge. Using insular time for study, self-development, and connecting to the higher self, knowing true intentions and purity of heart matter most.

cards.name: Tobacco
cards.up:
20. TOBACCO
​The guru
​Botanical name: Nicotiana tabacum
​Energy: majestic, detoxifying, and cleansing
​Other names: tabacca
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Fresh and dried leaves were historically used to ward off disease due to anti-fungal properties.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Smoked in rituals since ancient times to connect with spiritual realms; respected as a powerful plant spirit.
​The Poison: 
Falling for self-proclaimed gurus, spiritual charlatans, or leaders who exploit others' desire for growth for attention, profit, or control.
​The Antidote: 
Advises using discernment with spiritual teachers. True leaders lead with humility, empower others, and encourage personal growth rather than fear or dependence.

cards.name: Poison Ivy
cards.up:
12. POISON IVY
​Psychic vampire
​Botanical name: Toxicodendron radicans
​Energy: creeping, blistering, and tranquilising
​Other names: eastern poison ivy, poison vine
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Used in homeopathy for sprains and arthritis.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Carries protective energy and can be used in spells to block unwanted interactions or boundaries with others.
​The Poison: 
Describes one-sided relationships where someone constantly demands emotional support, rants, or asks for favors without offering reciprocity, acting as an emotional or "psychic" drain on others.
​The Antidote: 
Emphasizes that healthy relationships require mutual respect and two-way support. Encourages setting emotional boundaries and processing heavy feelings through journaling or therapy rather than dumping them entirely on friends.

cards.name: Cannabis
cards.up:
15. CANNABIS
​The healer
​Botanical name: Cannabis sativa
​Energy: healing and dreamlike
​Other names: bhang, ganja, hemp, marijuana, weed
​Traditional / Medicinal uses: Used to aid sleep, reduce physical pain, and ease discomfort.
​Magickal / Historical uses: Smoked in ritual settings to induce prophetic visions and connect with spiritual realms; misuse can lead to paranoia.
​The Poison: 
Points to getting stuck in a victim mindset or past childhood wounds, overreacting to challenges, or feeling overwhelmed by life.
​The Antidote: 
Involves doing necessary inner "shadow work," taking responsibility for one's life, and letting go of old wounds to step into a lighter, transformed role as a healer.

cards.name: Angels Trumpet
cards.up:
5. ANGEL’S TRUMPET
​Open your mind
​Botanical name: Brugmansia suaveolens.
​Energy: flighty and ethereal.
​Other names: angel’s tears.
​Traditional/medicinal uses: it was used in ointments as a pain reliever and anti-inflammatory.
